speechtext: This is a continuation of the same subject brought up some two or three months ago of unemployment of railway shop men. At that time it was decided that the situation would be met by a reduction of hours. However, all the shop unions met in convention at Vancouver and decided in favour of a continuous forty hour week instead of a reduction in hours. This of course means a reduction in staff. This is a matter entirely between the management and the union. Every possibility is being explored of putting additional work in the shop to justify added employment; nevertheless the management feel that under the agreement with the union they are bound to abide by the decision of the union, now that such decision has been arrived at with all the facts of the situation immediately before them.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in resuming the debate on the budget I may be permitted to express my sincere regret that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) is temporarily absent, and to express the hope that he will soon be able to resume the duties of his office. This incident indicates the stress and strain which is imposed not only upon members of the government but upon the leader of the opposition and other members by the political and economic conditions under which our parliamentary labours are conducted at the present time.
On the whole one must commend the budget speech of the Minister of Finance as

a clear presentation of statistical facts relating to domestic economic conditions and to Canada's economic relations with the United Kingdom and the United States; but we may differ as to several of the conclusions to be drawn from a careful consideration of these statistics.
The paramount value and importance to Canada of sheltered markets in the United Kingdom are made clearly apparent by the trade returns cited by the minister. For the fiscal year ended March 31, 1937, our exports to the United Kingdom were $406,825,443 and our imports $129,507,885 in value. For the fiscal year ended March 31, 1938, our exports to the United Kingdom were $407,797,610 and our imports $144,978,493. Our aggregate export and import trade with the United Kingdom in the two years ended March 31, 1937, and March 31, 1938, were:
Exports	$814,623,053
Imports	 274,486,387
Excess of Canada's exports. .. $540,136,666

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. I would ask hon. members to keep as silent as possible, in accordance with the rules of the house. It is very difficult to hear the hon. member who has the floor.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Surely a profitable trade with the United Kingdom to that extent should not be sacrificed by reason of any emotional or hysterical appeals for the improvement of our political relations with the neighbouring republic, as a basis for the establishment of peace throughout the world.
During the same two years, exclusive of gold, Canada's export and import trade with the United States was as follows:
Exports	$707,605,659
Imports	 881,049,642
Excess of Canada's imports . . $173,433,983
So in those two years, exclusive of gold, our trade with the United States showed a balance in favour of that country amounting to $173,433,983, as compared with a balance in favour of Canada in its dealings with the United Kingdom, for the same two years, of $540,136,666.
The existing trade agreement between Canada and the United States came into force on January 1, 1936. For the preceding calendar year 1935 the average ad valorem rate imposed on dutiable imports was 41-5 per cent in the United States, and from that high tariff level-the highest in the United States for decades, under the Hawley-Smoot tariff-the president of the United States proceeded to negotiate bilateral reductions in tariff rates under the conditions pre-

The Budget-Mr. Cahari
scribed 'by the United States congress; first, that no commodity subject to customs duty would be placed on the United States free list; second, that no rate of duty would be reduced more than one-half; and third, that the term of the agreement should be limited to three years.
The ad valorem rate of customs duty in Canada on dutiable imports in 1935 was only 27-4 per cent, so that in reducing the tariffs of the two countries percentage for percentage the United States ad valorem rate could be reduced to 20-8 per cent while the same reduction in Canada would leave an average ad valorem rate of only 6-6 per cent. So the president of the United States, from the beginning of these negotiations, has held the whip hand.
In the calendar year 1935, exclusive of gold, out of our total exports to the United States of $358,569,735 there were commodities to the value of $35,723,003 on which the United States customs duties were reduced under schedule II of the trade agreement which came into force on January 1, 1936. In the calendar year 1936, under the reductions made in the United States tariff, by schedule II of the existing trade agreement, these same commodities increased in volume in 1936 to $59,281,878, and in 1937 to $64,582,851, showing in two years, in respect of the commodities upon which specific reductions were made by schedule II of the trade agreement with the United States, a net increase of $28,859,858.
In the same two years, our total exports of commodities to the United States, on which no specific change was made in the United States tariff under schedule II of the trade agreement, increased from $312,846,003, in 1935, to $395,130,685, in 1937, an increase in two years of $82,284,682, thus showing conclusively that our exports of commodities to the United States, on which there was no specific change of duty, increased by $82,000,000, while the volume of our exports of commodities, on which the United States tariff was reduced under schedule II of the trade agreement, increased in the same two years by only $28,000,000. In other words, Canada fared more than twice as well in respect of exports on which there was no specific change in the United States customs duties than we did in respect of the volume of commodities on which reductions were made under schedule II of the trade agreement.
Canada's annual exports to the United States of commodities on which reductions in duty were made under schedule II of the trade agreement, increased foy $28,800,000, while the United States exports to Canada of commodities on which Canadian duties were reduced under schedule I of the trade agreement increased from $29,132,174 to $69,274,933, an increase of $40,142,759 in favour of the United States.
Taking the trade returns of Canada with the United States for the months of January, February and March of this present calendar year, 1938, we find from the finance minister's statement that Canada's total exports of merchandise to the United States were only $61,600,600, while our imports from the United States for the same three months period were $106,400,000, showing a trade balance adverse to Canada of $44,800,000 for the period referred to.
I commend the words of the finance minister, though they indicate a reversal of policy on the part of the Liberal party, that "Canada cannot give to-day and bargain to-morrow." And he added:
It is even more true, Mr. Speaker, in the world as it is to-day, that unilateral tariff reductions will not get the wider export markets which our products need.
We must not overlook the fact that there are bilateral trade agreements which are based on commensurate reciprocal concessions, and then there are trade agreements which are bilateral in form only, but the terms of which indicate merely the generosity of one contracting party in conceding tariff reductions without receiving compensatory advantages. The existing trade agreement with the United States is, in my opinion, of the latter kind, and I sincerely trust that all its adverse features may not be renewed.
In two years we obtained by our trade with the United Kingdom a credit balance of $540,000,000, while our trade with the United States showed a debit or adverse balance of $173,-
400,000,	which we covered by our exports of gold.
Moreover-
Says the finance minister, dealing with particular commodities-
-examination of exports of individual commodities to the British market for the last fiscal year as a whole shows such striking increases as 17 per cent in the case of bacon and hams, 33 per cent in the case of coarse grains, 86 per cent in the ease of tobacco leaf, 49 per cent in the case of fresh and canned fruits and 27 per cent in the case of iron and steel products.
The existing trade relations between the United Kingdom and the United States are not less unsatisfactory to the government of the United Kingdom.
It is stated in the Foreign Commerce Year Book for 1937, an official publication of the United States Department of Commerce, and
The Budget-Mr. Cahan

In closing, I wish to commend the statement of the finance minister that:
It is of little use to prime the pump of business enterprise with government expenditure, if, at the same time, we dry up the springs of private initiative which feed the well.
I was brought up in a country village, where almost every family depended upon its pump for one of the chief necessities of life. Pump priming was occasionally resorted to when the fittings of the pump commenced to loosen and to dry up. No efforts at pump priming ever increased the capacity of the well. The pump priming to which the finance minister referred should never be resorted to except possibly as a temporary expedient, but in any case its necessity clearly indicates the drying up of our industrial activities and the need for such remedial measures as will foster and encourage domestic industry.
Therefore I again heartily commend the following words of the finance minister:
If, therefore, the answers to the questions as to whether plants are to be built or extended, new houses are to be erected, and industry is going to expand or to stagnate, depend upon the decisions of tens of thousands of individuals who are free agents and not regimented sheep, it follows that governments must pursue policies which create confidence rather than fear and uncertainty, and which give leadership and guidance and encouragement rather than stifle initiative and paralyze new enterprise.
Therefore I am fully persuaded that if this government should maintain a stable monetary policy and adopt and pursue such stable trade and tariff policies as will create and maintain the confidence of the thousands of our people who are engaged in industry, then and then only will industry, and especially the manufacturing industry, so renew and extend its domestic activities as to solve for our time the problem of unemployment that now grievously perplexes not only the members of this parliament, but also the great majority of the Canadian people.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, every time it is my privilege to address this assembly in the budget debate I am filled with gratitude that long down through the ages someone has handed down to me the right to speak of the grievances of the oppressed in any part of Canada, and more particularly in my own constituency. I have also the further privilege of speaking favourably of the worthy budget recently brought down by a worthy man, a noble man who dares to do the right, but who is temporarily laid aside for a well-earned rest to resume, we all hope, his duties in this chamber in the course of a few days.

I am not going to carry on very long but I think I should say a word or two now lest I forget, about the two piffling amendments. One was well meant-I would not say anything unkind of the gentleman who is the financial critic of the opposition (Mr. Lawson) -but oh dear, how unlike the rugged, intrepid character of his present leader in this house, the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett)!
In passing I should like to say a word or two about the other amendment. Who will dare at this time to interfere with the buoyant revenues that we have available for taking care of the requirements of Canada? Does anyone think we could dispense with any of those revenues in safety at a time when the war clouds are hovering over us? Nothing but a piece of trickery was at the bottom of this subamendment. Do you think it will deceive anybody but the mover himself? It will not deceive me or my constituents or any sensible man in Canada. I despise such things on the part of men who pretend to be able to handle the affairs of Canada better than either of the old two parties. I hope I shall have a few minutes later on to deal further with the subamendment.
Now I come to another matter that I shall have to put on my glasses for. I hope I shall not need my auricular decorations but I have them on. I rather like interruptions, and I have a pair of ears beside me that will lend themselves to me to-day so that Hansard will not be full of interjections that I did not hear anything about. I do not think hon. gentlemen will do that, but it is well to be forearmed because I have had it done to me many a time.
In my morning paper, and you may be astonished when I tell you it is the Journal, I find the following extract, headed "Unable to say how many branch banks to close":
It is "impossible to say at this stage" how many bank branches are likely to close in Alberta, Sydney H. Logan, president of the Canadian Bank of Commerce, said to-day in commenting on yesterday's Calgary announcement that five branches will close within the next month.
"We will have to close more of them if we find the losses are too heavy. There are some small points out in the west where there is little business and the taxes make it impossible for such branches to pay."
Mr. Logan consulted records to show that of 221 branches 41 made profits and 180 were operated at an actual loss.
Well, I do not want hon. members to think what I am going to say is a brief for Mr. Aberhart. Heaven forbid that I should read a brief for that mistaken gentleman, but it is a brief against the president of the Bank of

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
Commerce or any other bank at this critical time adding fuel to the flames in our western province of Alberta by closing branch banks, no matter how desirable it may be economically to do so. It would be most untimely at this time; and who is going to say what will happen if it is done? The Bank of Commerce closed a branch bank in my home village last Christmas, and if similar arbitrary methods are employed, I am going to show this chamber what is now proposed to be done in Alberta. Go out into Alberta, forsooth, and start closing banks! An outrageously arbitrary act such as that of Mr. Logan in my riding and in my own village extended to Alberta at this critical time would be a regrettable incident the results of which no man can foretell. I hope there is some means in the hands of the government of restraining or at any rate guiding or controlling Mr. Logan, but I understand there is not.
Before I go further with this matter I should like to read a summary of the correspondence between myself and the same Mr. Logan-the most pinheaded, antediluvian bank president on the face of the earth, that I know of. I should also mention before I go any further that, because he would not give us a hearing, I told him "I will make you hear us on the floor of the House of Commons," and that is what I am endeavouring to do now.
Here is a summary of the correspondence. First, my own letter and my last to Mr. Logan:
January 15th, 1938.
S. H. Logan, Esq.,
President,
Canadian Bank of Commerce,
Toronto.
Dear Mr. Logan:
Yours of January 8th has been received, and I was glad to note that at least on one important point we have arrived at the same conclusion. In speaking of the last few years' excessive drought here, you say:
"We regard this, as you do, as temporary and expect that the district will return to its former productiveness."
What a contrast that statement is to that which you made in your letter of December 23rd, when discussing the same theme, as follows:
"The fact is that conditions have been changing greatly for the last ten or more years all over the west, and Abernethy is no exception. Volume and income have been decreasing for causes which seem to be permanent."
And then he followed that by saying that it is only "temporary." Well, Mr. Logan is certainly a lightning-change artist on manufacturing alibis.
This is only one more example of the rapidity with which you can change and vary your [DOT]excuses for closing our bank here.
As several of our lettergrams and letters have passed each other in transit it occurred to me that a resume of the whole disappointing occurrence might prove both interesting and constitute a consecutive record of the major facts of the case.
On December 15th, 1937, all patrons of the branch Bank of Commerce at Abernethy received the following letter from the manager thereof, with such variations in wording as individual cases necessitated:
"We regret to have to inform you that it has been decided to close our office at Abernethy on the 31st instant,"
That is December, 1937.
. .as our experience has shown that the volume of business offering in the district is not sufficient to warrant our remaining.
Unless we hear from you to the contrary in the meantime your account will be transferred to the Balcarres branch of the Royal Bank of Canada on the 31st instant.
Interest will continue on savings accounts without interruption.
We wish to take this opportunity to thank you for the business you have entrusted to us in the past.
Yours truly,
Manager."
That is, the local manager of the bank at Abernethy.
Although I am talking specifically about this branch, my information is that there are scores-I will not say hundreds, but there are many-similariy situated and, I understand, dealt with in the same arbitrary manner, throughout Canada.
Thus it will be seen that after doing a real good business at Abernethy since 1905 till the world depression and drought struck us and even a fair business afterwards, as crops continued wonderfully good, except in 1931 and 1937, when the major crop, wheat, was anything but a failure, as per figures already supplied you, we are to be ruthlessly deprived of our own bank with not as much notice given of your intentions as the most humble monthly labourer is entitled to before dismissal.
This real "bolt from the blue" resulted in a hurry-up telephone call being sent out over the ten rural lines converging on this point, announcing a meeting would be held the same evening to consider possible action to be taken to avert if possible, such hasty and unwarranted action, by remote control, as if your patrons had no more right to be heard in their own behalf than so many inanimate chattels.
The meeting was well attended by a stunned and increasingly indignant people. A petition was drafted addressed to yourself and largely signed, praying that no further action be taken looking towards closing our bank until patrons thereof had an opportunity to be heard and show cause why such drastic action should not be taken, at least until all the facts bearing on the situation were disclosed. Realizing that a reply to this petition could not be expected inside a week or possibly more, a committee of ten was named to interview your superintendent at Regina on Friday of the same week, as that was felt to be the proper course to pursue even though he (the superintendent),
The Budget-Mr. Motherwell

might have little, if any, say in the matter whatever. Which indeed proved to he the case as it did with ourselves afterwards.
Our interview with your Regina superintendent was quite frank and I would say satisfactory as far as it went, but it was quite apparent from the outset that the place to seek redress was higher up, as we had anticipated by addressing the before mentioned petition to you.
I addressed all these communications to Mr. Logan as did the local committee also.
Among other things we discussed with your Regina superintendent was the heavy overhead cost of operating the Abernethy branch, due partly to the capital cost of a much larger building than was necessary and the maintenance of a seemingly expensive staff. It was also pointed out to your superintendent that so far as collecting old paper was concerned, your then branch manager was a dandy, but so far as holding many old and valuable farm customers was concerned, _ he was a dud, owing to his haughty and high-hatting attitude towards them generally.
I pointed out to your superintendent that his manager at Abernethy was really a round peg in a square hole, inasmuch as he might make an excellent city banker, his total lack of rural instincts or sympathies was bound sooner or later to help to put any small village rural bank more or less on the decline by driving away good customers _ altogether, while others went elsewhere for their loans.
Between December 16th and 29th several further lettergrams and letters were exchanged in which, to support your determination to close your Abernethy branch, you stressed first, that the volume of income so decreased in recent years that there was no alternative to closing. To this I replied, in effect, that if every institution and business whose volume of business and income had shrunk were to be on fifteen days' notice closed up and deserted, there would not be much of anything left open and running.
I dilated on that in my original letter, but I want to emphasize it as much as possible. What would have been left running if every activity which showed declining revenues had been closed out? This parliament would have been out; the railways, the churches, all the best institutions of our land, our foreign missions included, would have been shut down and out. And yet this was the specious pretext made by this gentleman banker.
I followed this up with the actual shipments of wheat from this point as per railway figures for the years 1934-35-36; being 390,000, 250,000 and 354,000 respectively.
While 1937, the worst year we have ever had, the shipments of wheat thus far were about 120.000 with an estimated 20,000 yet to ship, and also 20 carloads of live stock. To this you came back with the unhappy plea that it was not the drought or yield or grade so much as the question of area-ours being too small in your estimation to support a bank.
Well, even a layman would know that it is the volume of business rather than th,e size

of the area which would be the determining factor. But this banking expert puts up an excuse that a third rate clerk would be ashamed to put up to try to satisfy us.
Surely, Mr. Logan, you do not expect anyone to accept that paltry excuse, especially as I showed you in one of my letters that our area had really remained permanent in that any little that had been lost by grain deliveries at Gillespie, most of which went through Abernethy branch bank, was more than made up by the accounts of the two rural municipalities, Abernethy and Tullymet.
Your faithful superintendent at Regina seemed to have acquired a premonition about this time that you needed some support on the theory that it was the area rather than the density of production and population that counted, as under date of December 28 he wrote me, from which letter I quote the following, wherein he intended to show that the area was over-banked;
"The Royal Bank of Canada having branches at Balcarres and Lemberg, while Indian Head cuts directly into the territory from the south."
That was the biggest whopper of them all.
This statement that "Indian Head banks cut directly into our territory from the south" is pure fiction. Prior to the construction of the Brandon-Bulyea-Regina branch line railway the farmers around where Lemberg now is and north thereof, also Abernethy and Balcarres and north thereof, practically did all their marketing and banking at Wolseley, Sintaluta and Indian Head respectively, but when banks were established at Abernethy and Balcarres in 1905 it cut so directly into Sintaluta and Indian Head banking area that the bank at Sintaluta was closed and the three banks at Indian Head were reduced to one, with the deep Qu'Appelle valley as a distinct boundary between them, thus lessening the bank competition from the south, instead of increasing it as alleged.
If this gentleman could get away with this kind of dope, well he deserves to; but as long as I have my voice and my general health to back it up he is going to hear from me. Talk about dictators; you do not have to go to Italy or Germany for them, we have *them right here in Toronto-and not Toronto particularly; we have them right here in Canada.
But why dwell upon all these-many of them petty and fictitious-alibis for closing down our bank when the real reason is given in your favour of December 28, in which, after reciting a number of other minor reasons why banks were being closed in the west and east also, you state as follows:
"In this present instance Abernethy was interlocked with other points, the Royal Bank and ourselves having arranged saw-offs involving nine places in all where a similar condition existed."
He must have thought that I was easy, when, our bank was valued not on the business that was being done but as a trade-off

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
for something else. Who could not be a banker if such qualifications as this went at par?
After all this pretence at reviewing and reconsidering the pending fate of our branch bank you now admit that it was all prearranged with the Royal that Abernethy was to be one of the victims of an admitted deal in which merit on our part made us all the more valuable as a pawn in your "saw-off" bickerings with the Royal.
I have nothing in the world against the Royal bank-
In fact I have nothing against any bank, but I have a lot against this loganberry banker who to our sad misfortune and mischance has apparently been raised to the high eminence of president of a great bank, the Canadian Bank of Commerce. I do not know much about banking; they have always treated me well, but I know this guy from the ground up.
-indeed I have had very satisfactory business dealings with it for many years, but to be bargained off to it or any other bank on a miserable fifteen day notice smacks altogether too much of the old massa and slave days of yore for a free people to accept with quiescent complacency.
Well, I am not going to accept it. Any man bom of Irish parentage on one side and Yorkshire on the other and who carries a Scotch name cannot be held quiet under such diabolical treatment as we have received from that bank president. Though the heavens fall I shall have my say. It is coming to me, not by privilege but by right. I gave them notice last New Years that it would come, and it has been fermenting here within every day since, waiting patiently to be let out, and out she comes now. There is more correspondence yet:
The always doubtful practice of "saw-offs" in dealing with election protests was quite common up to twenty-five or thirty years ago, but largely frowned down upon in more recent days. But with the Bank of Commerce at least saw-offs seem to be yet quite the right thing in determining which bank is to be continued and which closed, and with the same cavalier disregard for their patrons' interests as if they had been so many cattle.
Perhaps it shows disrespect to the cattle in making such a comparison.
At the beginning of this protest we did think that if we succeeded in presenting our case fully and had sufficient time to do it in, our branch bank with a business record behind it for thirty-two years which we have good reason to believe few village banks excelled, might yet be saved. But when we read your "saw-off" letter, we then knew what we had formerly only suspected, that our good old bank had not the chance of a corpse on the dissecting table.
Merit does not figure in it at all. Did you ever hear of such a condition of things?
Did you ever think that would or could happen in Canada? I did not; and when I awoke to the fact that it was there as a stem reality the Irish and the Scotch and the English in me rose to the highest pitch in my life-and they have had some rises. Now I am giving vent to my feelings, Mr. Speaker, at your pleasure. I had better hurry up, or the forty-minute time limit will be called on me. I wonder how many minutes I have left. Who is the timekeeper in this parliament anyway?
May I conclude by drawing your attention to your several references to our and my interview with your Regina superintendent. The reason we urged so strongly that either he or a responsible bank inspector should visit Abernethy was to meet your various customers at that point who had taken their bank accounts elsewhere, at some inconvenience to themselves, rather than meet your local manager personally and go through the nondiplomatic and repelling experiences to which hitherto they had been subjected. And these customers are some of our very best farmers in good circumstances, whom we desired your Regina representative to meet and size up for himself. But ye would not.
Yours truly,
W. R. Motherwell.
Well, there it is; and on inquiry I find that there is no official redress available and that the government has no power to act. I find that I have eleven minutes left. Heaven be praised; I feel like a new man, with all my garments on. But I am interrupting myself; I am full of appreciation of the kindness that has been bestowed upon me from all sides. I have a little more to say, but my few notes have taken wings elsewhere. I understand that there is no redress that can be accorded by the government or the parliament of Canada; in other words, this is a huge monopolistic banking institution-a free lance-to do as it pleases as above set forth. Through you, Mr. Speaker, I am going to address myself to the Canadian Bankers' Association. I want them to call off their dogs, to call off their autocratic presidents from entering Alberta at this untimely time. For fifty-six years I have been living in my farm home, building up the little village adjoining, and this is the sort of treatment I get from on high-not from on high; from below, from the depths of hades. Why should a man have his whole life-work interfered with by a ruthless bank outsider who knows nothing and apparently cares less about the rural areas of the country? Is it any wonder I am furious and indignant? And then there is no redress. I am addressing myself to you, Mr. Speaker, and through you to the bankers' association. There are many noble, fine, Christian men- not like this man-at the head of our banking
The Budget-Mr. Motherwell

affaire, and I feel that if they are appealed to they will see that some remedial action is taken. I am going to see that they get copies of this Hansard, I am going to see that it is sent to them, and I am going to depend upon them to correct this growing evil all over Canada. Is that not democracy? The Lord be praised for those who went before, who have given me this privilege of free speech on behalf of the oppressed.
I have only one further word to say, Mr. Speaker, to those who have listened to me so patiently. If the banks will not correct this-situation, what am I going to do? There is a great flexibility about our parliamentary system. I can remember when we had no law governing our grain trade; in that case the difficulty now is that we have a law but it is so difficult to get it carried out honestly. That, however, should not deter us from having a bank law and setting up a board of bank commissioners. Oh, that would be thought terrible. I suggested that to one or two in Ottawa, and I thought they were going to take a cat-fit. Why not? We have boards controlling almost all other institutions, and, in the light of the letter I read, who needs such control more than at least some of these banks? I am going to suggest to the Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister, and all the government, that they take into careful consideration the desirability of having a board of bank commissioners, so that when a bronco banker like this one breaks out, a snub twitch or a lariat can be put upon him. Do you think Canadians should have to submit to such tyranny? I do not.
I would be ashamed to think that Canada had degenerated to that extent. Freedom? Yes, there is a lot of nonsense spoken about it, but here is a real case where freedom has been usurped and authority flouted, almost equal to the case of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association with regard to farm implements.
That brings up another matter to which I should like to refer, since I have three or four minutes left, and it concerns the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), who is a very capable representative of that constituency. I only wish his capabilities could be turned to better purposes than pin-pricking annoyances such as this subamendment to the Tory amendment, which itself did not mean a thing. Neither the amendment nor the subamendment is worth enough paper to light a kitchen fire with, though if there is any choice between them the subamendment seems to be the worse. The hon. member wants to give away .all the tariffs that we inherited, which at the time of the Dunning budget of 1930 we had down to the lowest

point since confederation. He wants to give away all those remaining high tariffs which the present government inherited in 1930 with nothing in return from the United States. I want to use those tariffs as the basis of an agreement with the United States, in order to get something valuable in return in the form of more markets for Canadian products. That is the point. Is the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) not a good-natured fellow? A leader in agriculture wants to give away this chance. He says, "I do not want anything in return." Oh, Lord forgive him; he knows not what he says. How could he, when he would say that? Perhaps he thinks that would foe a cracker jack campaign issue to carry around. Well, I will see that it is not. I will spike it if possible before it gets out of the shell.
I think I have two or three minutes more, but perhaps Mr. Speaker will turn a blind eye to the clock this time. Speaking of shells: The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar is so anxious about agriculture and so anxious for immediate reform that he cannot wait a few months for one of the most wonderful proposals about to come out of its shell. I remember the early days, and the old reciprocity treaty of '54-'66. Why should I not be friendly towards everything that will promote trade between us and our southern neighbour- and much more so, the prospective trade agreement now pending between the United Kingdom, the United States and Canada, these three great democracies? But Mr. Rosetown-Biggar wants to give it all away for the purpose of doing a Little pin-pricking at the Minister of Finance. Ah, my dear young man, it will rebound on you, just the way the Saskatchewan musketeers drove the Aberhart invasion back into the lairs and kennels of the foothill country, and to the land of the breezy Bow. That is what we will do with the next invader. That is the way we will handle the C.C.F. at the first opportunity.
But this is not banking. I think I might very well terminate my speech right now. I could prolong it, but I am perspiring freely this hot day, and I want to retire to my drawing room and wardrobe.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with your permission I shall begin my remarks by paying a tribute to the whole population of the constituency of Berthier-Maskinonge, whose representative I have the honour to be in this house. I feel proud of those people, most of whom are farmers and. workmen, and I take pleasure in honouring them. I rise on their behalf in order to express their appre-

The Budget-Mr. Ferron
ciatioa of the Liberal government's achievements, and to make what they believe to be timely suggestions.
To be sure, in my constituency we are perhaps unable to juggle with figures as cleverly as the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lawson), but we do know that it is much better to strive after a balanced budget than to show huge deficits, as happened under the former government. We are no outstanding mathematicians, but we consider that we are not indulging in any whim when we prefer a deficit of a few million dollars to those of hundreds of millions which our critics have brought about and experienced.
Our knowledge of economics is still quite deficient; but we feel justified in stating that, on the whole, conditions have improved in every field af activity. Statistics show that unemployment has decreased to a certain extent in our country and, what is more comforting, confidence and hope are everywhere more noticeable. There is more confidence on the part of the farmer who acknowledges the goodwill which the government has shown towards him since they took power, in lowering to 7i per cent the duty on farm implements which formerly stood at 25 per cent. He feels more confident, as I say, because he knows that the different trade agreements which were negotiated have made it easier for him to sell most of his products; for instance, butter, which was selling for 22-8 cents a pound in 1933 and 24-7 cents in 1935, rose to 28-1 cents in 1937 and to 35-3 cents in February last.
Again, there is more hope among workmen who, in 1935 through the policies of our opponents, were under the threat of being discharged by the owners of the factories that employed them, for those factories would have to be closed, they said, if our party came into power. This we did, but those same factories are still in operation and giving employment to our workmen. In the case of the textile industry-a case in which the town where I come from is especially interested-it is now obvious, as a result of the inquiry which was held in connection with those companies, that they were not affected as they claimed to have been by our policy, but that they could pay better salaries to their employees.
The salary of men employed in lumbering and log driving operations has been raised because the market for forest products is now better than it was in 1935. Therefore we take pleasure in congratulating for that achievement, both the hon. the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) and the government of which he is a member.
After those congratulatory words, I am unfortunately constrained, Mr. Speaker, to make a few remarks and suggestions which might seem to border on criticism-which is not to my liking-but I am in duty bound to make them.
I will certainly support the budget on which we will soon be called upon to vote, but I should do it much more willingly if the millions of dollars intended for my province as a contribution towards the relief of the unemployed and needy were, in future, used more fairly than they have been in the past.
In 1936, and again last year, I had the opportunity of seeing the results of works done on the basis of cooperation. I am referring to projects 78A and 78B carried out in Louiseville, and to the Sainte-Genevieve road, between Berthier and Pointe-du-Lae. I did all I could to urge upon the authorities the principle of letting municipal councils choose workmen among the more needy of the locality, so that justice might be given to all, liberals as well as conservatives. Not only was my request turned down, but, on projects 78A and 78B there were foremen, or representatives of theirs, who did not hesitate to say to good unemployed labourers who wanted work in order to buy food: "You are not yet good enough tories to be given work here." The choice of workmen was made by political organizers, and I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the only thing about which they made no mistake was the political persuasion of the applicants. In spite of my protests, cases of political patronage and of glaring injustice have followed one another.
On the highway between Berthier and Pointe-du-Lac there have been injustices just about similar. In conection with that project, the Board of Railway Commissioners did something which, in my opinion, should not pass unnoticed. They found it expedient- I do not know for what purpose-to provide in conjunction with the Canadian Pacific Railway and out of moneys appropriated for the elimination of railway crossings, over 8400,000-that is nearly one half of the value of such work-after which they applied their unemployment relief conditions to about one third only of the project. As a result, almost all along that road, people in wretched circumstances were ignored so that employment could be given to political friends of the Quebec government. I ask again whether the Board of Railway Commissioners acted in good faith in that matter. If so, let me suggest that they are easily deceived.
The Budget-Mr. Ferron

Yes, Mr. Speaker, how much more willing would I be to vote these millions if, at least one half of that money was to be used a little more fairly.
As regards our old men and women, our unfortunate blind people and our youths, the vote of thousands and thousands of dollars will soon be sanctioned, so that their life conditions may be improved. I must say, that if, in this respect, the Quebec authorities deal with other parts of the province as they are dealing with my constituency, we may again expect numerous cases of abuse. There again, equal and fair treatment is unknown. Aiter having discussed the subject with the hon. the Minister of Finance, I realize how difficult it is for the federal government to interfere with such matters, but I wish to know if, after a thorough inquiry, such facts should not be brought to the attention, perhaps none too heedful, of the authorities in my province.
Mr. Speaker, dealing now with another subject, I wish to draw the attention of the hon. the acting Postmaster General (Mr. Euler) upon the rural mail carriers and to request his support on their behalf. I know that he is quite sympathetic to them and I hope that before long a reasonable and uniform salary will be paid to them, in spite of the difficulties which such action may involve.
Before I conclude, may I say a word about unemployment which, although less acute, is still existent. No class of the population has suffered more from the depression than the plucky labourers of our villages and small towns, where direct relief is unknown and cannot reasonably exist.
I have always been and still am of the opinion that governments should direct towards the land their efforts to end this sad state of affairs. Would it not be advisable gradually to reduce the grants for direct relief and transfer the difference to agriculture? But, let us not forget to begin by the beginning. We should in the first place seek to retain on the land those who are still there. We should strive to inculcate in the youth of the country the love of the soil, and the best way would be, in my humble opinion, to make grants for the encouragement of farm accounting. When books of account are kept in every farm house, the farmer's son will come to realize that farming is not what he had thought it was. He will be able to compare his income with the wages of labourers and factory-workers, with the salaries of store and bank clerks, and he will certainly find that farming is preferable to these other occupations.
Such a result, however, will not be obtained by conferences and fine speeches. It will

never be attained if, in the home, the child hears farming referred to only in words of disdain, and if means are not taken to make him find out for himself the truth of what I am advancing. He must be made to realize that the professional man without clients, the unsuccessful merchant, the unemployed workman may have to go without food, but that the soil of our country never withholds the means of subsistence from those who till it properly.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, let us direct our efforts towards the land. Let us seek to retain on the farm those who are there now, and their children. Let us try to return to the land those who have thoughtlessly left it, and the desired equilibrium will soon be restored. Let us not look for happiness in the newer and easier doctrines. God has said: "Thou shalt earn thy bread by the sweat of thy brow," and also: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself."
Let us rather return to the old doctrines which are and will ever remain true. If we always preach them and practise them, happiness will assuredly return to every Canadian home.

Practically every dollar of that revenue will be obtained from the common people. They pay the customs duties and the sales tax. They pay the excise duty, because that is added by the manufacturer to the cost to the consumer. They pay a large part of the income tax. The estimated grand total revenue is put at $501,700,000. Such a statement should not be applauded; it should be looked at with a great deal of dissatisfaction. We expect to get that much revenue this year, and yet the deficit is put at $13,775,000. That means that we are going into debt that much more. There is another thing that should be mentioned because we heard so much about it a few years ago. It was said that conditions were going to be so much better and the Liberals were going to make it their earnest endeavour to bring about
that state of affairs. When we compare the budget of last year with the one of this year we realize that there is something like $62,538,000 more to be collected. It is not very consoling when you realize that that increased amount will have to be taken from the people in the form of taxation. It will mean a lower standard of living, and the people are certainly not going to be content when they see their standard of living being lowered year after year.
We see the results of this all over the country. We saw it in Vancouver and in Winnipeg, and it is evident in Ontario. A thousand men have been laid off in the Canadian National Railway shops in central Ontario. If nothing is done, these men will be organizing themselves into unemployed strikers. We will find the same thing spreading over the whole country. These men will be forced to organize and when they are organized they probably will be able to obtain some results. That is what will happen if we keep on in this slipshod manner. The main and supplementary estimates this year call for total expenditures of $524,600,000. This amount, which included the expected deficit of $13,775,000, will either have to be collected from the people or borrowed. If we borrow the money, then we must pay interest. Our national debt at the present time is over $3,500,000,000. I intended to bring down with me figures showing the increase in the national debt from the year 1912, but I am sorry I have not them with me at the moment. The gross debt in 1912, as I recall it, was something like $483,232,000, and on that we paid roughly $12,605,000 of interest. Out of every dollar of revenue collected there was about 7-7 cents required to pay interest on the debt. In 193637 the debt had increased to something like $3,542,000,000 with a total amount of interest of $137,410,000 and we had to pay for interest 30-30 cents out of every dollar of revenue collected. That is a tremendous amount to pay for interest. There must be some end to this ever increasing debt. In order to raise the necessary money we had either to borrow directly from the banks or to float loans. I had intended to bring down figures on that this afternoon, but speaking from memory, the cost of these loan flotations ran into millions and millions of dollars every year. Included in the expenses of the flotations were travelling expenses, bank fees, solicitors' fees, brokerage fees and many things of that nature. This is something which the government should take into consideration, and which they promised to take into consideration in the election campaign of 1935.
4182	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
I noticed when the budget speech was being delivered that there was a great deal of applause from the Liberal benches when it was stated that interest rates had been slightly reduced. It is quite true that they have been reduced, and the government deserves commendation and encouragement in that respect. In that connection I want to read from page 3902 of Hansard, where the Minister of Finance said, speaking of the interest rate on the debt:
On the other hand the average rate of Canada's debt outstanding as at March 31, 1931, was 4-98 pe"r cent, and to-day the corresponding rate is 3-53 per cent, a decrease in the ease of Canada of 29-1 per cent.
That is very commendable, and as I say, the minister's statement brought a great deal of applause from the Liberal benches. That is one thing that should be carried further, and I should like to make this point:	If
the rate of 4-98 per cent was too high and we were able to lower it to 3-53 per cent, why not lower it still more? True, 3-53 per cent is better than a higher rate, but the evil is only lessened in a small degree. I think we should recognize that fact and be consistent in our thinking and reduce interest rates, as we in this group have advocated on every occasion, or eliminate interest entirely; because there is no logical reason for borrowing money and paying interest on it. Rather, as was said by the Prime Minister in his election speeches, we should issue money in terms of public need.
At page 3903 of Hansard the Minister of Finance makes a statement in which he ridicules the contention of the social crediters that debt free money should be issued. He said:
There are some, of course, who appear to believe that the government should not pay interest at all or, indeed, should issue debt free money to finance its expenditures or to retire its interest-bearing debt, or to do both of these things. It is incredible that this hoary fallacy should persist after so many historical demonstrations of its devastating possibilities.
The Liberals thought it was all right to reduce the rate of interest on the debt from 4-98 to 3-53 per cent, and yet the Minister of Finance condemns those who advocate issuing debt free money.

speechtext:
No, but there was no doubt to whom he was referring, because he looked straight over here and said

that for the last two or three years this fight had been going on. Listen to this and we will see if there is any doubt about it:
The government is of opinion, after watching developments during the past two years, that it is highly undesirable and very much against the national interest that there should be continued political controversy with respect to the constitution of the bank itself. It is for that reason that, in addition to maintaining the control which t'he government now has through a substantial majority on the board of directors, the government should acquire the whole of the ownership of the shares of the bank. This has been suggested on more than one occasion by members on all sides of the house, and the government hopes that it will dispose once and for all of political discussion relating to the constitution of the bank itself.
Political discussions! I am afraid the political discussions will not be stopped merely by the nationalization of the bank. While that is very commendable, and I have no bone of contention to pick with the minister in that respect, the mere nationalization of the bank will not do what the voters intended should be done when they voted the Liberals into power. It was not only the nationalization of the bank that they asked. What they asked for was the issuance of currency and credit in terms of public need, and as the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) said the other day, everyone expected that that was to be done, not by borrowing, but by issuing our own money and credit. But that has not been done. This party has consistently stood fast by the principle of nationalization of the bank if nationalization was necessary. We have supported that and have no dissatisfaction with that proposal at all. We think that if it was necessary it was the proper thing to d,o. But we contend that mere ownership is nothing, that unless the bank is controlled and directed by parliament then all talk of democracy is idle and futile. These words were never more true than when they were spoken by the Prime Minister himself. The Prime Minister listened, I think, very intently to the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard speaking in this house the other day, and acquired a great deal of knowledge he never had before in regard to banking. It is not only the Bank of Canada we have to watch, but the chartered banks. They are the ones who control the issue of money. They are the ones who are responsible to a great degree for the poverty that exists in this country. These conditions are not due to any lack on the part of the producers, manufacturing, or agricultural, because we have an abundance. Those are responsible who sit in control of finance, and who are

The Budget-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
now very highly lauding the budget that was presented this year. They are the ones who are responsible, and they should be made to answer directly to parliament.
The unemployed, when they read the budget will find small consolation. They will realize that this government intends to do little for them. Certainly the thousand men who were laid off the other day from the Canadian National shops will not, when they read the budget, find in it a great deal to be proud of. The men in Vancouver, in Victoria, in Winnipeg, and those who were in Calgary not so long ago, will find nothing whatever to look forward to, but everything to their detriment, when they read over this budget. Some of them get a small relief allowance, part of which we immediately take back from them in the form of a sales tax, increased to eight per cent, on everything they buy with the proceeds of that allowance. If -they buy sugar they have to pay an added tax; on almost anything which they buy they have to pay excise tax or custom duty or sales tax or some other kind of tax. In that way their standard of living is being continually lowered. I think this is a matter to which we should give the most serious consideration. Now is the time to do it; we should no-t wait until there is a recurrence of what has just happened in Vancouver.
I am astonished that the government has not given more attention than it has to the situation of these unemployed young men. The other day I received a letter regarding a young fellow who, married two years ago, had steady work and just managed to get by until a few months ago. His mother wrote to me and asked, "What is he going to do? He is out of work." I personally know this man; he is as fine a man as I have ever met, a personal friend of mine. Yet he is going to be in the class of those unemployed men who are now striking. Can you blame them? All they are asking for is a chance to work at a decent wage. I do not suggest that strikes or relief riots or any action of that kind will get them what they desire, ibut I say that we down here are the ones to blame, we are the ones who should shoulder the responsibility, and if we would do what the Liberal party said they would do, issue money in terms of public need, one of our greatest difficulties would be overcome.
I believe that when the farmers review the budget they, too, will not have very much ground for satisfaction. It is true that they have been granted a little reduction on 51952-265
gopher poison, but all the gophers were poisoned before the budget came down this year, so they have not much to look forward to in that respect; and next year probably the tariff will be changed. Then there is a reduction on harness. But in the west harness is becoming obsolete; the farmers are using tractors, but there is no reduction in the duty on tractors or on farm implements. This is one of the matters to which a great deal of consideration should have been given. We had a committee sitting here for I do not know how long, investigating the prices of farm machinery. They brought in a very good report, yet nothing has been done.
On the whole the budget is a great disappointment to thousands upon thousands of the Canadian people. So far as I can see, the only ones who will benefit from it directly or Indirectly are those who are in control of finance, those who are continuously making huge profits, running into millions of dollars each year, out of interest rates. I notice that the interest rate was cut. I also noticed in the return-I am sorry I have not it here-that every year without exception the amount of money we pay to the bondholders on our funded and unfunded debt has increased. It is all right to lower the interest rate as we have done. But on the other hand our national debt has increased so that we have to pay more money by way of interest each year. That is a thing which must stop. When people cheer the reduction in interest rates they do not know what they are doing. If they look more carefully at the return which was brought down in this house they will find that they are paying more money out of revenue in interest than was ever paid before, because our national debt is going up faster and higher than the interest rate is being lowered.
I do not intend to take much time, because I know the house is anxious to get through with this debate. When the Bank of Canada bill comes down I should like to see a great many changes made in it, so that the common people of this country will be given a chance, so that the young men and women who are depending upon work for wages will have a decent chance of a livelihood, that they will have a Canada of which they may well be proud. Although the budget has not provided for it, there can well be provided in the Bank of Canada bill what the Liberals promised, namely, the issuance of credit and currency in terms of public need.

The other cause of the spread of these movements in Canada is the determination of the capitalistic classes to continue to enjoy their high dividends and excessive profits at the cost of the sacrifice of the great masses of the people who work on the farms and in the factories and who are to-day having such a struggle for existence. I refer to the great army of honest toilers, struggling under serious disadvantages and making great sacrifices for those dependent on them, denied the advantages, many of them, of a proper education, and robbed of many of the necessities of life, while others live in luxury and enjoy the wealth which the toilers have produced. This has been proven by many investigations which have been made during the past number of years. If ever a dictatorship form of government should come to Canada, the moneyed in-51952- 265J
terests carrying on under this system of grefed and selfishness would be one of the direct and principal causes of its coming. There are no truer words than those of Burns, who said;
Man's inhumanity to man
Makes countless thousands mourn,
I have been very much interested in the discussions in this house from time to time with respect to farm problems. One thing on which I am sure we all agree is the fact that we cannot have prosperity in Canada unless the farming industry, the basic industry of Canada, is placed on a profitable basis. We must admit that it is far from that to-day.. I have heard many suggestions in this house' as to what wouid help the farmers, such as, reduced tariffs, reduced taxes, reduced transportation rates, freer access to the market's of other countries, and so on. These will help, but to my mind neither any one of them in itself nor all combined will'solve the farrti problem. The farm problem will never [DOT] be solved so long as farmers continue to work under their present system. Farmers must learn to do their own business, and not depend on others who are virtually conducting [DOT]the farming business to-day, not for the benefit of the farmer but for their own benefit and profit. Why should not farmers own their cheese factories, their creameries, dairies, cold storage and packing plants, abattoirs? The farming industry will never be on a profitable basis as long as private interests control [DOT] the sale of farm products. This must be removed from the control of private interests and a system of cooperative buying and selling adopted, a system which ; is working so satisfactorily in such countries as Denmark and Sweden. This cooperative system was not easily brought about, but followed a long and continuous struggle with the moneyed interests who fought so hard to prevent the farmers from getting together in a cooperative movement. This has been the history of every country where the farmers 'have undertaken to organize for the purpose of working co.-operatively in any branch of the farming industry. In this regard Canada has been no exception, and our Canadian farmers, in undertaking cooperative organization work, must be prepared for a long, continuous struggle; for it will take some years to bring about this cooperative farm movement unless the government will come to their assistance; which I am hoping it will see the necessity of doing. If the farmers of countries such as I have mentioned can make a success of the cooperative farm movement, as they have, surely there is no reason why the intelligent farmers of Canada cannot make a success

I am thoroughly convinced that there is no way in which the government can be of more assistance; in helping solve farm problems than to encourage the farmer with financial assistance so that he may become properly established.' in a cooperative marketing system. When the control of the marketing of farm products is taken out of the hands of private interests and operated in the interests of the farmer, then, and only then, will we have a satisfied and contented farm population in Canada. Then we will have something to attract the young and rising generation to the farms instead of crowding into the cities, as they are doing to-day, and our farm problems and to a very great extent our city relief problems will be solved.

Let us endeavour to people our country as it should be, lest we too fall a prey to the covetous eyes of nations who are not so favourably situated as we are.
There is another aspect to the farm problem about which I wish to speak. I often wonder if those who are not engaged in farming ever realise the position that agriculture holds, relative to the other industries that make up our economic system. Let me use a simple illustration, so simple that I feel like offering an apology for it, but I know of none better and so am going to use it to serve my purpose. It is nothing more than a direct application of the underlying principle of all business, which at some time or another is applied to adjust prices by the various industries that make up the round of our industrial life. Might I ask hon. members to indulge their imaginations for a short time and think of me as a farmer raising hogs on an extensive scale?
Some years ago, just before a sharp rise in freight rates took place, I sold a carload of hogs to be delivered two weeks hence f.o.b. shipping point. In the meantime the increase in freight rates had gone into effect. When the meat packer received the hogs he found his freight bill was up $50, and likewise the freight on all his other shipments of hogs was up corresponding amounts. He immediately gets busy and says, "Here, my hogs are costing me more money; I must have more money for my products." He marks up his prices accordingly. He passes on the increase. He sells his products to the retailer who receives them over the same transportation system. The retailer finds that his invoice is marked up, as well as the cost of his freight or express. He gets busy and says, "My goods are costing me more; I must mark up my prices." He marks them up accordingly and passes on the increased cost. A housewife comes in for her weekly supply of foodstuffs and discovers that prices are up. When she goes home she says to her husband, "I will have to have a larger allowance next week because I find that groceries and other necessities have gone up in price." Her husband meets with his fellow workmen to talk over the matter, and finally they decide that since their living costs

The Budget-Mr. Fumiss
have gone up they must ask for more wages. Their employer being a reasonable man, he grants their request. They pass on the increased cost to their employer.
Suppose this employer is a manufacturer of farm implements. When he looks over his payroll he discovers that it has gone up ten or fifteen per cent. He says, "My labour costs are up; I must mark up the price of my implements," and he does so accordingly. He passes on the increase.- I may need a new set of implements -the following spring. When I interview the agent I find that prices are up fifteen or twenty per cent. As I must have the implements I buy them. If the cost of my implements is -up, I must have more money for the next car of hogs I send to market. However, when I try to pass on my increased cost, what happens? I am just as likely to have to take less for my hogs as I am to get more. I am lucky if I break even in a comparison with the previous year's prices. That is the position which agriculture occupies as compared with other industries in our country. Farmers to-day are working eighty, ninety and one hundred hours a week for less wages than the urban worker receives for a forty-four hour week. That is why people are leaving the farms and flocking to the cities.
With our present system there has to be some industry -that bears the burden of any readjustment in prices. In our case that industry is agriculture because it cannot count any increased cost of production as a factor in setting its selling price. I have taken you around -the circle and shown that even though agriculture has not contributed to the increased cost, yet it has had to bear that additional burden. I had to pay the additional cost for my implements, but I had no way to recoup myself. That being so, then the only thing that can be done is to make -the burden as light as possible. I complain only of unjust burdens, and I named the most vicious -one when I referred to high tariff protection. There are many others which I shall not attempt to mention, but let me say here that I consider anything for which no value is given as an unjust burden.
I would refer particularly to profits on watered or common stock which do not represent a single dollar of cash investment. One has only to refer to -the Turgeon report on the textile industry, or to the report of the committee on agricultural implements, for glaring examples of this. I might refer also to the artificial prices placed upon real estate for which no value is given, but which must be paid by some person. These are some of the burdens that eventually have to
be borne by the farmer. Until they are removed from our system, our farmers are doomed to be hewers of wood and carriers of water for the other organized interests in the country.
One other way in which agriculture can be helped, is in the marketing of its products. Hitherto the activities of our departments of agriculture have been along the lines of increasing production, but I am pleased to see that, the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has initiated an aggressive program of marketing. I trust that this will not stop short of assisting in the cooperative processing of our live stock. We have one plant fashioned after -the Danish system which is operating successfully in Ontario at the present time. I believe this is the only solution to be found for the problem which has been referred to this house on several occasions.
There are other things about which I should like to speak in connection with my constituency, such as reforestation and the tourist trade, but they must wait for another occasion.
Just a word about the unemployment situation. I have listened -to many speeches in this house with regard to unemployment, and I have come to the conclusion that some people think all this government has to do is to wave a magic wand, say "presto", and the problem of unemployment will vanish overnight. This problem has been too long in the making to be cured in one year, in three years or in ten years. For tens of years the best brains of the country have been employed in the discovery and invention of labour destroying machines without a single thought being given to the effect on our economic system. Now our best brains will be required for many years to find a way out of this difficulty in order that we may maintain our individual freedom and our democratic form of government.
Let me, say in conclusion that I do not believe man can create any condition which he cannot redeem if he sets himself diligently to the task of finding out the cause and resolutely applying the remedy. That is the task which confronts not only this country, but every other nation- in the world. If this problem cannot be solved, then civilization as we know it, is doomed to perish.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a certain degree of trepidation that I rise in my place in this house to make a few remarks on the budget that was presented to the house last Thursday. I must say, Mr. Speaker, at the outset of these brief words how deeply I feel for the absence of
The Budget[DOT]-Mr. Fleming

the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) from this house on account of illness. The. Minister of Finance is one of my oldest and closest personal and political friends. I have known him intimately from my early years in Saskatchewan. He has always given the best of his time and his energy for the welfare of his adopted country. I hope that his recovery will be rapid and that he will soon be back in his place in the House of Commons where he occupies a position of such eminence in this new country.
I was pleased as I sat here and listened to the fine exposition of the Minister of Finance concerning the financial affairs of the country. I listened also with considerable pride to the degree of improvement that has been made in our financial position during these difficult, trying, and troublesome times. The financial management of the country has been good, but I was dumbfounded when I found no measure of relief in the way of tariff reductions for the people of the western plains and the people of the constituency that I have the honour to represent in this House of Commons. I must offer, in my humble way, my protest.
I returned just a short time ago from the election battle in Saskatchewan, and during that campaign I addressed, with my fellow-members of this House of Commons, a great many meetings. At these meetings men and women of all shades of political thought and political beliefs were gathered together to listen to the problems to be discussed, and at all these meetings I found that the people we were addressing were one in asking for some relief from the troubles they were enduring. I personally addressed some thirty-five meetings in the time I was absent from this house, and the one question that was uppermost in their minds was that the government of Canada should do something to alleviate in some small way the distress under which they were labouring. At nearly every meeting questions would be asked, and the question that was always asked was: What is your government going to do in the way of removing duties on agricultural implements?
I told them that if they would be reasonable; if they would wait for a short time, I was sure that when the budget was presented this year some measure of tariff reduction would be contained therein. I told them that it was a Liberal government under the leadership of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, in 1911. that brought to them the first measure of tariff reform. I told them that it was the Liberal government under the leadership of

the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that brought, in the Dunning budget of 1930, the second great measure of tariff reform to the people of western Canada.
But many of these people asked this question: Why do they wait until election year to do these things? I, in my implicit faith in Liberal governments, in Liberal policies, in Liberal doctrines, said to them: Send Liberal representatives to the parliament at Regina who will foe in favour of lower tariffs, and if you do this I can return to my place in parliament and say with strong united voice: "Lower those tariffs, Mr. Dunning. We still trust you. We still believe in you as one of Saskatchewan's great premiers."
But, Mr. Speaker, when I find that nothing has been done in the matter of tariff reductions on farm implements or on anything else, it is difficult for me to support a policy of this kind. The Liberal party had its rise in the natural impulse of the people toward greater freedom, and in all its history it has never lacked witness to the fundamental truth which that word has come to mean. Liberalism means more to me than a passing fancy. I have always believed that in the Liberal party there was the greatest measure of freedom of thought and freedom of action. But the other day, within the hallowed walls of this house of parliament, I happened to ask for some information from one of the ministers of this government, and he turned upon me and said that this Saskatchewan bunch was so-and-so, and that he would not support the wheat board if we did not support the budget. Mr. Speaker, let me tell this house, and let me tell this government, that as long as I am a member of this House of Commons I will not be intimidated by any minister of the crown. I come from a race that has never admitted defeat. For seven hundred years the Irish people fought the might of imperial England, and I as a member of that race will never be coerced by any ministerial threat, whether it comes from privy councillor or governor. This is supposed to be a democratic government, and no party whip will snap me into action.
I resent the intejection that was made during this debate a few days ago by the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Fraser), when he said in a sneering way that we, the members from western Canada, would vote for the budget. Let me tell that hon. member; let me tell this house; let me tell this government, and let me tell this country, that I believe in the Liberal policy and in the Liberal platform. I believe in a united

The Budget-Mr. McGeer
Canada. Too long have we, the people of the western plains, been sacrificed upon the economic altar of St. James street. I believe in national unity; I believe in confederation, and in a strengthened confederation at that, but I believe that the conflict between dominion and provincial powers has reached a point where we may have to decide between a strong federal government and a redivision into provinces and sovereign states. Personally I believe that national unity is essential. Western Canada has contributed much to our national unity and to our national economy.
I mentioned in a former address in this House of Commons that we had been discriminated against by transportation rates and by tariff walls under various federal administrations, but that we had never openly advocated secession. We have always relied upon the good will and understanding of other parts of this great Canadian country which have profited by the new markets which the development of our western lands has opened up to them. But we have now reached the point when something must be done to help the people in those great areas of western Canada. Whatever may be the outcome of our difficulties, I am confident that our destiny lies in confederation, and I am convinced that the way leads through the Liberal party. If there ever was a danger to the west's position, it is through that political appendage of industrialism, the Conservative party.
I cannot vote for the amendment, nor can I vote for the subamendment, because one would mean a Conservative policy, and the other would mean that in order to bring those things into effect it would have to be done through a Conservative government, and we know what that would mean because it is the party of higher protection. The socialist or Cooperative Commonwealth Federation amendment is simply adding a few words to the Conservative amendment, and it in no way modifies or changes the Conservative amendment.
Mr. Speaker, we are an intelligent people. If we gave as much time to the consideration of the broad principles of distribution of the benefits of our progress as we do to much squabbling over inconsequential items of routine administration, the people would have more confidence in us as their leaders. Let us face the future fearlessly. Let us walk with dignity and with pride into the future. Let us believe in the character of our people. Let us believe in the legitimacy of our dreams. Let us return to the principles of Liberalism, those principles that were taught to us by the great leaders who have gone
before, those principles of orthodox Liberalism that I learned at my mother's knee. I think, Mr. Speaker, the government should promote a policy of the technique of transition :-
So in the long hereafter this Canada shall be The worthy heir of British power and British liberty-
Spreading the blessings of her sway to her remotest bounds,
While with the fame of her fair name a continent resounds;
True to her high traditions, to Britain's ancient glory
Of patient saint and martyr alive in deathless story,
Strong in her liberty and truth to shed from shore to shore
A light among the nations-till nations are no more.
Mr. Speaker, after thinking the question over, after communing alone with myself, I have decided that there is no solution that I can offer to this problem which I have been debating with my inmost self, but that I must support my own distinguished leader the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King) and will vote for the budget.
