speechtext:
May I tender my regrets and message of sympathy to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) in the unfortunate break in his health at this critical time? I sympathize with him the more because I feel that under the course which he is following it is utterly impossible for any Minister of Finance to retain his own health, much less the health of the public purse of the nation.
We have been listening to budget statements for a great many years, and they are all attended with a great deal of justifiable optimism. Apparently that optimism must come from the fact that "hope springs eternal in the human breast," because on every single occasion, whether openly acknowledged or ingeniously concealed, our budgets have consistently shown a deficit that has continually mounted as the impossible and unpayable debt burden of the nation.
If you examine this budget, Mr. Speaker, you will find it strangely similar to every other budget which has ever been introduced in this house. It indicates the persistent rise in the ever-increasing dominion, provincial and municipal taxpayers' load of debt, which is now over $7,000,000,000. The fact is that the Conservative party was elected in 1930 on a promise that they would cure unemployment with an appropriation of $20,000,000 of public funds, and that our national debt has increased by over $1,000,000,000 since 1929, and is still increasing without any real solution being offered of the unemployment problem
The Budget-Mr. McGeer

in Canada, notwithstanding some measure of success. Why is it that a nation as rich as Canada cannot have progress without that progress being overshadowed by unpayable increases in existing unpayable debts? To-day, notwithstanding that the budget shows the highest revenue ever collected in the history of the dominion-and similar expressions are coming from cities and municipalities-investment in city property from one end of Canada to the other is practically a liability. Under the blight of existing taxation business in Canada has come practically to a standstill. Our public service lags far behind twentieth century standards, and unemployment not only continues but is again rising.
I do not want to be one who has not hope for the future. But I read to-day that in the Canadian National Railway shops some thousand men are being laid off until the fourth of July, and Mr. Kingsland, one of the vice-presidents, announces that we shall have to w'ait until then to see what is going to happen. In my own province of British Columbia we had hopes that the war in Asia would not last very long and that there soon would be a revival of Asiatic trade. To-day, as a result of there being little or no hope of an immediate conclusion of that disastrous conflict across the Pacific, some industries have been hit with almost the same force that the drought conditions struck the farms in southern Saskatchewan. I suggest to the government that it will be a serious mistake for this house to rise without some more ample provision being made for the emergency possibilities of unemployment during the coming year than exists at the present time. It may be unfortunate, but I understand that neither Ontario nor Quebec is willing to cooperate in guaranteeing the loan which this government has made to municipalities for the purpose of preventing unemployment through the promotion of self-liquidating enterprises at a two per cent rate of interest. I know there is no possibility, with the amount of money which would be our share in the province of British Columbia and in the city of Vancouver, of meeting the problems that I feel reasonably satisfied we are going to face before the coming winter is over.

speechtext:
Before recess I had drawn attention to the fact that under our present system progress seems to suffer under the inevitable stalemate of debt. But worse than

that, every sane person must acknowledge that a system which taxes us into depression and prevents progress and prosperity, where there is every reason for believing that prosperity and progress both can and should exist, does not contain the remedy for the most important of all Canadian problems, namely that of financing greater Canadian expansion and development, and more widespread and general prosperity. The time approaches when we must all come to the conclusion that our present and previous budgets indicate that those who have the responsibility of administering public affairs must give much more real thought and study to theories and practical details of monetary policy than has been the case in the past. If there is one outstanding feature of our whole economic program to which public men, whether they be in municipal life or provincial or national life, give little or no attention, it is the actual details of our monetary system. Such thought would go very far to disclose that the root of much of our present economic difficulty will be found in our overcautious attitude towards public administration of national currency and credit. We seem to be afraid as public men to grasp and take hold of that all-important problem. Worshipping at the shrine of orthodox finance we ignore the truth that our government is poor simply because parliament has given away its power to create money to those who have made the cost of financing government prohibitive. The result is that while the government exerts great and ingenious efforts to balance the budget, a little thought would disclose that in reality it is vainly trying to budget on a balance. That is, we are trying to budget the affairs of the nation on the inadequate balance of the nation's money power which the taxpayers can afford to borrow from the private hoardings of accumulated savings and from the owners of our privately owned credit system.
The absurd and impossible situation of being taxed into depression exists simply because we have followed the thoroughly unsound proposition that sovereign governments have no access to public spending power other than by collecting taxes from and maldng other levies on the people and by borrowing from accumulated savings. That this proposition is thoroughly unsound is no longer open to question. Ever since the Minister of Finance for Canada has acknowledged that we in this country have adopted a monetary system based on "a managed paper standard" under which "the value of our currency is determined by the principles of demand and supply," we in parliament, by the adoption of that

The Budget-Mr. McGeer
policy, have made the lawmaking authority of parliament the source of supply of Canadian money. Therefore, unless the government has given away its power to create money through law, or does not know how to manage national currency and credit in the service of the nation, parliament has the power to create and circulate the medium of exchange in the volume that is needed to sustain Canadian progress with orderly advancement. Unfortunately we in parliament have given away, not to the Bank of Canada but to the chartered banks, the power to create Canadian money. Surely every member of this house and every citizen of Canada must, at one time or another during the last few years, have asked himself or herself, From what source are other nations securing the power to finance progress to the extent that it is being financed in other nations, as well as to finance what is unfortunately more costly than progress, the enormous war programs which are under way in practically every nation in the world? This parliament, due to its affiliation with the League of Nations has a right to review what has been said by the director of the international labour office at Geneva. He summarises the world situation in these words:
But perhaps the most outstanding lesson of the slump is to be found in the profound change it has produced in ideas about monetary policy. In this field more than in any other lies the key to economic prosperity and social progress. The demonstration that in one country after another the upturn of business and employment coincided not with the reduction of wage rates, the cutting of costs or the deterioration of working conditions, but with the abandonment of deflation and She adoption of monetary expansion, has made a deep impression on the world.
Surely this experience the world over proves that the time has gone by when men can acorn controlled inflation and monetary reform and dismiss it idly as something unworthy of consideration. Nations the world over have found a new lease of national strength and new recovery of internal prosperity in the management of their own currency, the acceptance of this conclusion is not dependent upon the evidence which may be found in the monetary experiments of the dictatorships, Russia, Japan, Germany or Italy, or in the pump-priming program in the United States, although the successes and failures of their fiscal policy should not be ignored; for such countries, bankrupt a few years ago, irrespective of whether they are using their financial resources effectively or otherwise, are no longer short of money. People say -that the Roosevelt program of
expenditure has failed. Let me ask any member of this house what would have happened in 1933, 1934, 1935, if the national government of the United States had not undertaken such expenditures. Even to-day those who scorn Roosevelt's attempt to conquer poverty for the people of the United States are-forced to acknowledge that if the national government of the United States failed to go forward with a further spending program, the inevitable result would be a disastrous depression of unparalleled dimensions.
But quite apart from the dictatorships or the Roosevelt administration in the United States, there is ample evidence to support the significance of monetary reform to be found in the recovery program of the British isles, where under a completely revolutionized monetary outlook, human and national need policies are being projected and financed upon entirely new theories of financial and political economy. The epochal British revolt against orthodox finance and classical economy was engendered by sheer necessity, and arose directly from the failure of the deflationary policy launched in 1925 by Winston Churchill, the then chancellor of the British exchequer. Under that policy Mr. Churchill hoped to restore international -trade and, in turn, internal trade in Britain by reducing public expenditure, salaries, wages, working conditions, living standards and the cost of industrial production, accompanied by whatever increases in taxation were necessary to balance the budget. Under that misguided policy, which I am afraid we are continuing to pursue in Canada, the national credit of Great Britain was almost destroyed. The resulting collapse of her national credit and security forced -the British government to repudiate orthodox finance and classical economy and stake her whole future on inflation.
What has happened in England is simply this: The government has taken the control of currency and credit away from irresponsible bankers and placed it where it properly belongs, under responsible government. From the point of view of human well-being this revolution against banker rule is just as important as and more far-reaching than Magna Charts; for through it the government has found the means of financing the public services that are essential to orderly progress. The old days of laissez-faire are over in England; the day when the government can be indifferent to industry and the wellbeing of the people has passed. Now the British government moves to protect the standard of living of the humblest and to
The Budget-Mr. McGeer

guard and protect industry in all its ramifications. The first great step in the emancipation of Britain from the slavery of orthodox finance has been taken, and other steps are certain to follow; for this money revolution in Great Britain was not born of blind selfishness or class hatred but had its genesis in the evolution of intelligent understanding. It has been fostered by outstanding industrialists, the London Chamber of Commerce and men of high finance such as Reginald McKenna, war-time Chancellor of the exchequer, who financed the war on a managed currency basis. As chairman of the Midland bank, on January 27, 1934, he laid down this basic rule for all governments to follow:
Nothing in monetary practice is more certain than that contraction of the volume of money, or even failure to secure an adequate increase, tends both directly and indirectly to put a brake upon business of every kind, and to produce the very troubles-unemployment, unremunerative commodity prices, unbalanced budgets and general depression-which have been apparent in almost every country of the world in the past four years. "With expanding population and production we need expansion in the supply of money, or it will inevitably follow that consumption will not keep pace with production."
The support of McKenna for the new British policy was quickly followed by the endorsement of John Maynard Keynes, who pointed out:
The creation of legal tender has been and is a government's ultimate reserve; and no state is likely to decree its own bankruptcy or its own downfall so long as this instrument remains at hand unused.
Thus we accept Mr. McKenna's contention that an expansion of credit is the key to the situation. But we conclude that if whilst an increase volume of bank credits is probably a sine qua non of increased employment, a program of home investment which will absorb this increase is a sine qua non of the same expansion of credit.
What we have done in Canada is to create an abundance of credit, but we have not provided that adequate program of home investment which puts that accumulation of credit to work for the Canadian nation and the Canadian people. This problem of public spending presented by Keynes is in reality the one that the British government has solved, and I think it has been solved in this way. If the people owning savings fail or refuse to exchange their savings for treasury notes or other governmental securities offered on terms fixed by the government to provide the government with funds needed for new enterprise or to balance the budget, then the banks are called upon to absorb such securities by expanding bank credits which are placed at the 
disposal of the government in the form of bank deposits. Therefore the British government always has at its disposal a plentiful supply of money on its own terms. By investing such credits in social services, public works, the development of trade, and the national defence, the British government is able to keep circulating the medium of exchange needed to increase the production, distribution and use of wealth, to raise the standards of living of the people, to enlarge the national income, to increase the volume of trade and the stability of commerce, to supply the means of paying taxes, to maintain all public services and to make more secure the defence of the United Kingdom and its world-wide interests. The British government, by spending national credit, is now fulfilling "its most conspicuous and sacred responsibility," namely that of supplying the circulation of consumers' buying power which is the economic blood-stream of the commerce and industry of the capitalistic democracy that it is charged to sustain.
In avoiding the evil consequences of inflation the British government first limits its expenditure to what it thinks are the practical, economic, social and national needs of the day. It also maintains a scheme of high and widespread taxation on income which prevents the accumulation of an excessive volume of issued buying power medium of exchange. It also maintains a definite leadership in the regulation of prices, wages, working conditions, production and distribution, taking particular care to prevent the development of speculative booms in securities and commodities. Expenditures on social service in Great Britain are no longer feared as burdens of the state but are now being recognized as essential not only to those in need but to the general going-concern activity of the business of the nation. For the same reason the British government now spends freely in granting financial aid to housing and slum clearance programs; to shipping and industry; to the development of electrical energy; to the recovery of fuel oil from coal and the nationalization of coal mines; to agricultural production and, through other channels, to all phases of national development.
Under this practical perspective of currency management the British government now meets the entire public cost of unemployment relief, unemployment insurance and health services, old age pensions, mothers' pensions and aid to children; and through grants in aid has assumed much of the liability of the poor laws and many other obligations which formerly fell upon the taxpayers in counties and municipalities. In pursuance of her policy of relieving the owner of improved property under

The Budget-Mr. McGeer
local government from the burden of excessive taxation by local authorities, the national government Of Great Britain now pays some sixty per cent of the cost of education and fifty per cent of the cost of local police services. In addition to these continuing obligations she goes forward with a tremendous program of national rearmament.

speechtext:
Now that my right hon.
friend has raised that question, let me deal with it. In addition to pouring out money for those in need through her inflationary policies, she is also able to pour out, to those who have accumulated savings, an income via the interest route; but if my right hon. friend will be patient for a little while, I shall deal with the reason for that and I think he will agree with me, because probably he knows more about it than I do. But there are men in the old country who agree with me, and I am going to quote one now. For instance, in connection with the controlled inflation program of the British government, in his annual statement to the shareholders of his bank in 1935 Mr. McKenna pointed out that the adoption of controlled inflation was the first essential to the recovery of British commerce and industry, and he then stated:
The quantity of our money is no longer governed by the fortuitous supply of gold and the degree to which hoarding is practised by central banks and others. The quantity of money is subject now to pure management with first regards to the needs of commerce and industry.
I venture to say that the experience and record of the Right Hon. Reginald McKenna, both as chairman of the Midland bank and as chancellor of the exchequer place him in at least as high a position of authority as that held by the right hon. leader of the opposition in the Canadian House of Commons.
In the May 21, 1938, issue of The Economist, which I have no doubt the right hon. gentleman reads, we are also told:
There are distinct signs that the policy of aheap plentiful credit is being continued and intensified so as to combat the recession, and also so as to facilitate the financing of rearmament. Such a deduction is not at variance with the occasional reaffirmations of monetary policy which from time to time have emerged from official quarters.
That the British system of managed currency is directly under the control of the government was positively declared by Mr. Neville Chamberlain, then chancellor of the British exchequer and now Prime Minister, in his address at the Mansion House on October 7, 1936. On that occasion he stated:
Sterling is still free. It is unlinked to gold or any other currency. There is no alteration in the credit policy which is necessary to preserve the internal prosperity of this country or of the other countries of the British empire. "Our improvement is principally due to two causes, both of which arise directly out of government action. The first is the system of very moderate protection which we have established, and the second is the maintenance of low rates of long term interest. We have not in contemplation any change in either of these two branches of our policy."
Here is the chancellor of the British exchequer taking full responsibility on the part of the British government to regulate the rate of interest on long term credits in the British isles. When I mentioned this fact to the house the other night I thought it well to quote it again, because it impressed me so much. I believe I have nearly committed it to memory. When I heard the governor of the Bank of England acknowledge that the government had the unqualified cooperation of British bankers, and that the government was in complete control of the money system, I was amazed. However these are his exact words:
Those for whom I speak welcome the freedom which we have in comparison with those in many other markets, but we wish to use that freedom in the only proper way it can be used, and that is in harmony with the government's policy. I assure the ministers that if they will make known through the appropriate channels what they wish us to do in furtherance of their policies they will at all times find us willing with good will and loyalty to do what they direct as though we were under legal compulsion.
Here is a British chancellor of the exchequer declaring a policy of government control, and the head of the Bank of England, speaking on behalf of the bankers, declaring that "we, as bankers in England, agree with that program."
The Budget-Mr. McGeer

We have a little different attitude in Canada because the statement of the governor of the Bank of England stands out in marked contrast to the statement of the deputy governor of the Bank of Canada who, speaking on March 28 in Ottawa to the junior board of trade, said:
In many countries the policy of the government [DOT] is the policy of the central bank; certainly no respectable central bank would accept a policy from its government with which it differed fundamentally.
Of course that was the rule when Mr. Osborne was imported by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) from the Bank of England to come to Canada to run our bank; but it no longer prevails in any respectable democracy; for now in respectable democracies the governments and not the bankers rule the nation's currency and credit. British economic and national power to-day gives final refutation to those who have parrotlike repeated the shibboleth that a nation cannot spend her way to prosperity and security. Proportionately to her population, national income, wealth and debt load, Great Britain is spending annually not as much as Germany or Russia, but slightly more than Roosevelt is spending annually in the United States, and at least double the amount we are spending annually in Canada.
If Great Britain were to reduce her budget to the basis we have adopted as safe and sane for Canada, she would cut her annual expenditure in two. What would be the result? Her national defence would be destroyed; her foreign trade would be lost, and her internal economy would stagnate in a welter of bankruptcy, destitution and revolution. We would have conditions in England such as unfortunately we have to-day in Vancouver.
The present plan of Great Britain may be criticized as being far from perfect. I know they are still borrowng unnecessarily, and I know they are still paying interest unnecessarily, but it can be said -that much of the public financing has been reduced to the lowest rate of interest in history, and the government is in control. But the great thing about British policy is that Great Britain is no longer short of money. It .must be remembered that this new plan is only seven years old. It dates from the bankruptcy of Great Britain in 1931, when she collapsed under the gold standard, orthodox finance and classic economy.
It must also be remembered that it is being carried out by a government which represents the Conservative minority in England whose respect for the wages of money is still higher than its regard for the wages of men, and 
whose worship of the institutions of accumulated wealth overshadows its concern for the well-being of individuals other than those possessed of interest bearing bonds, and those who live by the sweat of other men's faces. What a great thing it would be for this Dominion of Canada if the right hon. the leader of the opposition would take as much interest in the wages of men as he takes in the conditions of those who collect interest on government bonds 1
To the government may I say this, that continued indifference to the financial needs of provinces, cities and people, and to Canadian progress, prosperity and security will not command the respect of the majority indefinitely, who I believe are beginning to feel that the time has come when we should be moving along the lines of currency management which other nations are successfully developing.
^ Along the course of controlled inflation that Great Britain has taken to success we in Canada must not be afraid to follow; for through her new' monetary system developed under the British empire currency policy of 1933, to which Canada is a party, Great Britain now has billions for unemployed relief, pensions, education and other social services; billions for reconstruction of home and city; unlimited billions for the promotion of trade and commerce and the maintenance of empire defence, and billions for the betterment of the world at large.
How is it that that little country, with her limited natural resources, her tremendous obligation to maintain the value of her buying power in the world's markets, and in view of the relation she has to import trade, can do all she is doing under managed currency, when we still are afraid to move-with . so little done, so much to do and so much to >
do with? There is no reason why Canadian development cannot go forward in the light of the experience of other nations, which demonstrates the facilities that can be used for development.
What I wish to point out to the house is this, that we have adopted inflation, and we adopted it under the right hon. the leader of the opposition, when he was Prime Minister, at the time when he put into effect the British empire currency policy at the Ottawa conference in 1932. That was the development which followed the collapse of the world economic conference in London of that year. We adopted that policy first in 1930, second in 1932, and then what did we do in 1933?
To make it effective in our dominion coined gold was withdrawn from circulation; the right of the free export of gold was cancelled; -the

The Budget-Mr. Bennett
price of gold was raised from S20 to $35; the right to secure the conversion of paper money and bank deposits into gold on demand was wiped out, and we established a virtual government monopoly over the purchase and export of gold. The issue of a stabilization fund of $250,000,000 to maintain the international value of our dollar was authorized by an act yet to be proclaimed, presumably because our favourable balance of trade has been so satisfactory that it was not necessary, which is a fact.
In 1934 parliament, recognizing the need for currency and credit expansion in Canada, which the new policy contemplated, enacted the Bank of Canada Act containing provision for the reduction of gold reserves for currency purposes to 25 per cent, and it also provided for the complete suspension of gold reserves by order in council in case of national emergency.
Parliament also amended the Bank Act to permit chartered banks to create and issue bank deposits on a five per cent reserve of Bank of Canada bills. By these laws this parliament reduced currency and bank deposit legal reserves and extended the limits of inflation so that our banking system could provide the government with the use of the nation's credit in almost unlimited volume. Parliament in addition did everything necessary to permit our banks to extend to our dominion, provincial and civic governments the plentiful supply of money that a managed currency system is designed to supply, which, under public control of currency and credit, is now available to the governments of Great Britain, Germany, Italy, Japan, Russia and many other nations.
The cardinal features of these laws, which every member of parliament should know if he is performing his full duty, are very simple. They are to be found, first, in section 26 of the Bank of Canada Act, 1934, which permits the Bank of Canada to issue full legal tender money on a 25 per - cent gold basis, which means that it can expand gold into four to one of legal tender currency. This section gives the Bank of Canada the exclusive right to issue all Canadian full legal tender cash in the forrp of currency bills and, as I said a moment ago, on a basis of expansion of four to one.
Under section 27 of the same act, and under subsection 4 of section 59 of the Bank Act, 1934, the chartered banks are authorized to issue bank credit in the form of alleged bank deposits on a five per cent reserve of Bank of Canada bills. Therefore, for every five dollars of Bank of Canada bills which the Bank of Canada may issue, our chartered
banks are authorized by parliament to create bank credit in the form of bank deposits up to the value of $100, which they can create with a bookkeeping entry and use to purchase government bonds and securities. While these enactments hardly justify the statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) in this house on March 8-

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not rise to address this chamber on the budget. I had intended to make a few remarks, but on account of the regrettable absence of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), which I trust will be but for a very few days, I shall defer what I have to say until his return. My remarks would have to do with questions connected with the balance sheet as presented the other day, and I shall not trouble the house in that regard at this time. However, I desire to make a few observations with respect to the amendment to the amendment which has been submitted by my hon. friends to my left.
I well recall the circumstances under which the present Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) so brilliantly and powerfully sought the support of the electors in western Canada on promises that were not unlike those contained in the 1919 platform of the Liberal party. Those of us who recall the election of 1921 and the attitude of the Progressive party of that time with respect to matters mentioned in the subamendment, as well as the attitude of the present government in the presentation of its platform, will well remember the picture that was painted as to what was to happen if they came into power. They succeeded in 1921. The subamendment directs attention to the fact that they disregarded the pledges contained in their platform of 1919, of two years previously.
I am bound to say that I cannot find it possible to express regret that they did disregard their pledges. I rise merely for the purpose of directing attention to the fact that it is hardly fair to blame those of us who opposed that platform and who pointed out

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
what would be the inevitable consequences of its being adopted in practice, if we do not to-night give our support to that subamendment. It will be a matter of curious interest to us all to observe the attitude of some of those who assisted in the preparation of that platform. Many of them were not members of parliament at that time, but there are many who attended the great convention of the Liberal party held in this city in 1919 at which that platform was prepared and at which those promises were given to the electorate. We did express the view that if those promises were given effect to; if they were promulgated in the form of policies; if they were enacted as statutes, the result would be disastrous to Canada. It is a matter not of regret but of satisfaction to know that those who now sit upon the treasury benches have seen fit, as evidenced by their conduct, to admit that the position which we took was sound and that their promises were made, shall I say, in error.
There remains, therefore, nothing for us to do but to dissociate ourselves from the amendment to the amendment; not to express regret, but to express our pride and satisfaction that the government, by reason of their appreciation of conditions having recognized that to have given effect to these pledges would have been disastrous to the nation, have seen fit to do the exact opposite. They have thereby given my hon. friends to my left an opportunity to ask those who promulgated those promises publicly to express their disapproval of the promises they made and of the platform they promulgated by voting against the resolution which expresses regret that they have not kept those promises.
Mr. Speaker, I repeat that I rose merely for the purpose of expressing, not regret that the promises made were not kept, but satisfaction that they were not. Despite all the promises that were made and the speeches with which this country was deluged; despite the literature that was spread from one end of this country to the other; despite the votes that were secured and the great and powerful campaign carried on by my hon. friend who was the leader of the then Progressive party, he now finds 'himself associated with the government in forgetting those promises. I congratulate them warmly upon this state of affairs. I congratulate the country upon the fact that we have a government with, shall I say the courage to disregard its promises, with such a high and fine sense of its responsibilities to the people as to forget these pledges were ever made and to wish that they had not been made.

I believe that the group in this corner are following the policy which we have used for many years, that of voting with any group which states our ideas, so in a moment it will not trouble us at all to vote with the Conservative party.
May I point out to the Prime Minister -what he may not have noticed-that the Conservatives have just voted with the Liberals; or, shall we put it the other way, that the Liberals have just voted with the Conservatives?

speechtext: Any thoughtful person in Canada has known for a long time, certainly since that marvellous speech the Prime Minister made on the night of the election of 1935, that we have one great Conservative party in Canada. It is true that it has two parts, one called Liberal and the other called Conservative. But it is quite obviously a conservative party, with a small "c." Many people in Canada, and possibly many in the Conservative ranks, are somewhat worried over the lack of success of the Conservative party throughout Canada. May I point out to the Conservatives in this house that the reason why they are not more successful is that Canada does not need two Conservative parties. Having one that is so overpoweringly successful, we do not need another. As a word of advice and encouragement to the Conservative convention about to convene, I would say that the only way I see that they can attain power is by becoming liberal, because Canada certainly stands in need of liberalism. The group in this corner has stood by the ideas in which they believed in voting for the Liberal platform of 1919, a platform the principles of which have been reaffirmed by Liberals many times since 1919.
