subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I was paired with the hon. member for Northumberland, Ont. (Mr. Fraser). Had I voted I would have voted against the motion.
Notice should have been given in votes and proceedings because this amendment will have material effect upon the exemption provisions.

It does. The first paragraph of the amendment deals with structural steel. That is simply an addition to the list, although it is important. The second paragraph provides for the exemption of articles which enter into the manufacture of building material, and is a very important provision. I hope it will not be necessary to delay consideration of this by reason of the addition of these two items. I would suggest that since this applies only to the exemption of building material, and since there are a few other changes in the Special War Revenue Act which come before this, we might deal with the others first. The first item is, "Materials for use exclusively in the manufacture of gopher poison."

I think, Mr. Chairman, that would be an admirable way in which to take the resolution.
Materials for use exclusively in the manufacture of gopher poison.

Gopher poison as a finished product has been exempt from sales tax for some years. No provision, however, was made in respect of the materials used in its preparation, although the ingredients constitute the main item of expense in making gopher poison. Administrative difficulties in the past have made it impossible to effect the exemption in respect of ingredients inasmuch as they were purchased from so many different sources, and at times through retailers possibly many times removed from the manufacturer of the ingredients, who under the law is responsible for this portion of the tax. The manufacturer was not able in most instances to certify that any particular portion of, say the strychnine sold, found its way eventually into gopher poison. Recently it has been found that more than 75 per cent of the gopher poison used is of one brand, and this concentration of supply makes the exemption administratively feasible.
Item agreed to.

Special War Revenue Act
Harness for horses and complete parts therefor and articles and materials to be used exclusively in the manufacture thereof.

Farming machinery generally and farm equipment of many specified kinds are exempt from sales tax, and it is found that this general exemption might properly include harness. It has been estimated that about 95 per cent of all harness made is used by farmers, and accordingly the exemption is made general rather than limited to the particular use by farmers. Parts and materials used in making harness are also exempt from sales tax, following the existing practice which obtains in respect of parts, machinery and equipment and materials.
That would include buckles and copper rivets?
Yes.
And the wax ends used in sewing, I suppose?
Yes.
I have been asked whether it would include collars. Should not also the wording of the item include mules, which are used in some places quite extensively for farming?
I am informed that it is construed as covering harness for mules.
If that is so, all right. I just wanted to know.

Item agreed to.
Feeds for fur-bearing animals whose pelts have commercial value.

The existing exemption in respect of animal feed specifically mentions fox feed. Calf, cattle, hog and poultry feeds are also exempt, and the specified list of particular kinds of stock feed are exempt. Under the existing wording, however, no exemption is allowed in respect of feeds for fur-bearing animals other than foxes, as for example, minks. To remove this ambiguity it is proposed to allow an exemption in respect of feeds for all fur-bearing animals whose pelts have a commercial value.

That was what was
originally intended, anyway.

Item agreed to.
Articles and materials for use exclusively in the equipment or repair of boats used by fishermen in the fisheries.

At present an exemption exists in respect of ships licensed to engage in the Canadian coasting trade and in respect of boats purchased by individual fishermen
for their own personal use in the fisheries. Furthermore, materials used in the construction, repair, or equipment of ships are exempt, also articles and materials used in the manufacture of boats owned by individual fishermen for their own personal use. It will be noted that with regard to these exemptions no mention is made of articles and materials used in the equipment or repair of the boats. This is an anomalous situation, and the proposed amendment removes the anomaly by extending the exemption to cover all articles and materials for use exclusively in the equipment or repair of these boats.

This was asked for by the fishermen on the Pacific coast, principally the small boat owner. They will appreciate the amendment made. I should just like to have it made clear that the boat will not have to be registered to get the benefit of this exemption.
It will not.

Item agreed to.
Bricks; building tile, building blocks and building stone; plaster; lime; cement; stucco and stucco dash.

The amendment which I have proposed adds structural steel to the list of building materials. Structural steel is in competition with cement, and since cement was in the list it seemed to toe desirable to add structural steel. Then came the question about the materials that enter into the manufacture of these exempted building materials. If they had not been added to the list, it would have meant the tax would have been transferred from the finished building materials to the taxable elements which enter into their manufacture, and that would have reduced the effective exemption from eight per cent in some instances to a considerably smaller amount. Since the budget was presented last Thursday, a great many representations have been made by persons interested and others, from which it was apparent that serious administrative difficulties would arise. For example, a manufacturer who manufactures taxable building materials and materials [DOT] that hereafter would be exempt from sales tax would find it very difficult to separate the raw materials into those which were to go into the tax exempt finished product and those which were to go into the taxable finished product. That is one of the administrative difficulties which arises, and for that reason and others it was felt desirable to add this to the list of exemptions.
Special War Revenue Act

It means, of course, that the eight per cent will now be completely removed without deduction for the tax on the materials.

Mr. Chairman, with respect to the item dealing with bath tubs, et cetera, not including pipes and pipe fittings, it means that the accessories to the various items mentioned here will pay the tax, even though they may be chromium plated, whereas the bath itself and the shower will be free from tax. Is that a sound provision having regard to the fact that we are now dealing allegedly with the construction of homes? It must be remembered that we are supposed to be making exemptions here to help the man who is building a house, and clearly there are pipes connected with the introduction of a bath into his home, some of them chromium plated but coming under the head of pipes, because a bath tub as it comes from the factory has no accessories attached to it at all. Before it is put into place you attach the various accessories; very often nowadays they are plated with chromium. But as this item reads, even these pipes would not be free from the sales tax.
There is this further point to which I desire to direct the minister's attention. After all, structural steel does not enter into any cheap houses. Structural steel has practically nothing to do with the kind of houses we have been discussing, and the provision regarding it cannot be taken as any incentive except where the larger construction in cement does touch the smallest and lowest priced house. I can understand the desire to make the items complementary, and the action is thoroughly understood in that regard. But when you come to say, " articles and materials to be used or consumed exclusively in the manufacture or production," you have all this machinery. Take, for example, the grinding of white lead. What are you going to do about it? These articles are used exclusively for that purpose. I do not think the minister had that in mind, but surely that is what it means in a court of law where ultimately it would have to be construed.
Articles and materials to he used or consumed exclusively in the manufacture or production of the aforementioned building materials, but not to include materials consumed by waste or wear or abrasives, lubricating oils, fuel oils or non-permanent plant equipment.
"Non-permanent plant equipment." You see it does not include non-permanent plant equipment; therefore it would include permanent plant equipment. That would be the construction which I know the minister would say should be put upon it by a judge. The
[Mr. lisle;'. 1
very fact that it does not include non-permanent means that it does include permanent. I did not see the amendment until a moment ago, but I do not think the minister had in mind the machinery used, for instance, in grinding white lead or in preparing linseed oil. I notice that the words " paint oil " are used. That, of course, involves the use of an inferior product instead of what has usually been the standard product in connection with matters of that kind, but I take it the minister had good reasons for doing that. The cheaper oil makes an inferior paint. Linseed oil is used in the higher standards of paint, white lead being the basis of it. The minister, I am sure, does not mean to free the machinery, shall I say, or any parts of it that are permanent in their character, from the sales tax. I am not quite sure, but I think the clause is drawn in such a way as to leave it open to an ambiguous construction.
The wording is that at present used in the act to cover materials, and it has not before been argued, although the-
The necessity has not arisen.

-right hon. gentleman has
argued it very well, I think, that " articles " may, perhaps, literally taken, mean machinery; "articles ... to be used or consumed exclusively in the manufacture or production" of these products has always been construed by the department and held to mean materials or something that actually goes into the product, and not the machinery, and the reason "non-permanent plant equipment" is inserted is to make it clear that this non-permanent plant is not included under " materials."
I realize that.
It is often argued that nonpermanent plant of certain kinds is material.
Oh, yes, I know.

That is the reason for
that.

I realize fully why that
is inserted, but I dii'ect attention to a possible ambiguous meaning of it.

It is now suggested that
when the words "non-permanent plant equipment" are used, an implication arises-
The minister is an excellent lawyer, and he remembers the rule of law that if you mention the one you exclude the other.

Yes. There is no objection
to putting it beyond doubt by saying "nonpermanent or permanent plant equipment."

Special War Revenue Act
Yes. I think that would overcome a possible difficulty.

I think it is better to put
both words in than to leave both out.
Quite. One or the other.

Unfortunately we have no copy of this amendment or any information about it at all except what we have heard read. I may be wrong in what I have caught from the words of the minister. Might I suggest that instead of using the word "articles," the word "materials" or "ingredients" should be inserted, because that is all that is involved. It is materials or ingredients which enter into the manufacture of these things, and obviously not an article that is used in the manufacture; yet the amendment, I understand, says, "articles to be used."
Before the minister answers me, may I point out this, which I gather has been considered by the minister in the last few days. I understand, as regards this list of items entering into the construction of houses, building construction, the resolution as it is at present drawn will create a chaotic condition among those who are manufacturing these articles. I notice the minister referred to subseqent items in this group, so I shall also do so. Take for instance:
Builders' hardware, namely: locks, lock sets, butts, hinges, pulleys and window fasteners.
Have representations been made-I understand they have-by the manufacturers of these goods, and, if so, have they been given full consideration? I am informed that if the resolution passes in its present form, it is going to create a serious condition, the objection being that under the law as it has been worked for many years the original parts which enter into a finished article are not taxed at all, but the finished article is taxed. Now, if the finished article is exempted, it leaves the manufacturer of the primary part taxable. That, of course, was never intended. I do not think the amendment will correct that situation.
It is intended to.

I have just received a
*copy of the proposed amendment. It reads:
Articles and materials to be used or consumed exclusively-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I do not want
to interrupt the hon. member, but I think, to keep the record clear, this amendment should be read. It has not yet been read from
the chair, and it has been suggested that there should be some change. It is moved by Mr. Power:
That paragraph 1 of the said resolution be amended by adding at the end thereof the following:
"Structural steel to be used exclusively for the framework and support of building and bridges.
"Articles and materials to be used or consumed exclusively in the manufacture or production of the aforementioned building materials, but not to include materials consumed by waste or wear or abrasives, lubricating oils, fuel oils, permanent or non-permanent plant equipment."
Quite-"permanent or nonpermanent."

I do not wish to seem to quibble over this matter, but as I read the proposed amendment it refers to building materials. What does that include? Would it not be necessary to classify under one group all the materials affected by that proviso? There is one item here:
Bricks; building tile, building blocks and building stone-
And a number of items, all of which go into buildings. Am I to understand that this amendment will apply to all those items?
Yes.
Does the minister think that is sufficiently clear?
Yes, it will be placed at the end of a paragraph containing that list.
I suppose that will appear clarified in the bill?
Yes.
Is the minister satisfied that this completely covers hardware, for instance?

No; only the hardware
named.
Builders' hardware, namely: locks, lock sets, butts, hinges, pulleys and window fasteners.
It covers locks, lock sets, butts, hinges, pulleys and window fastenings, and the materials going into the manufacture of those are exempted now by the amendment.
Will that include, for instance, screws and bolts-

No; it does not include anything except that named in the list. It does not include all builders' hardware but includes only the builders' hardware named in the item.
Special War Revenue Act
In looks there are a certain number of screws.
If they are included in the locks, they are exempt.
It will include those?
Yes.

It is claimed by manufacturers that this will introduce an atmosphere of confusion impossible to overcome. I simply wish to be assured that this point has been considered by the department officials and the minister and that they are satisfied that this amendment will meet the situation.
Yes; those representations were received and carefully considered, and the amendment will, I think, do away with practically all the difficulty anticipated by the manufacturers.
Will that cover furnaces for heating?
Furnaces are listed.
Furnaces for heating buildings only.
Furnaces for buildings are exempt, but the raw material that goes into those furnaces, that is the steel, was not exempt. Now that will be cleared up?

Yes, exactly.
Mr. MeCULLOCH: Is sewer pipe to connect the building with the sewer exempt?
No; pipes are not exempt. That is not building tile.

The hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Gladstone) has a letter here which covers the situation to which I have referred. In the plant with which I am connected we manufacture the steel boilers that this heating firm uses, and I am interested in this.
This clearly covers furnaces for heating purposes only.
Yes.
That is, boilers of all kinds?
No; furnaces, not boilers.

Information has come to me from a circular that may have gone out to the customs officers giving a list of goods exempt from tax; "hot water and steam boilers, cast-iron and steel, used for heating buildings; bungalow heaters used for heating

buildings; warm air furnaces, steel or cast-iron;"-and then this note: "Note carefully: materials used in the manufacture of exempted items formerly not subject to tax are now taxable."
The amendment changes that.

In heating buildings with hot water or steam, a boiler is an essential part of the heating equipment. A building could not be heated by steam or hot water without a boiler. I think the question raised by the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Gladstone) was whether the boiler would be exempt under the amendment.
If it is part of a furnace, it will be.
The boiler is certainly part of the heating equipment, but I do not know whether they call it a furnace.
This does not cover heating equipment; it covers only the furnace for heating purposes, and that has a well known trade meaning.
For the provision to be effective with regard to heating equipment it would surely be necessary to include the boiler that goes with the furnace.
Not all heating equipment is exempt. For example, radiators or stoves are not exempt.

Practically all buildings of any size that are being constructed to-day use either hot water or steam heating. I cannot see why a steam or hot water heating plant should not be exempt as much as a hot air furnace.
All I can say is that, if it is part of the furnace, it is covered by the amendment.

I have not been able to get a copy of the amendment; therefore I cannot tell what is exempt. Is expanded metal, wall sheeting, metal sheeting, metal roofing, flashing and sheet metal that would go into a cheaper house or a farmer's bam included?
If the hon. member will name those articles one at a time I will tell him.

Expanded or corrugated metal for sheeting, galvanized iron and tin and sheeting used in the construction of houses and bams.

Special War Revenue Act

When used as siding or
roofing they would be exempt.

Just a moment ago we
were speaking of furnaces, and I was wondering if this should not include cooking ranges, for this reason: In some of the smaller houses they have not made provision and perhaps will not make provision for furnaces. About all that such houses will have will be cook stoves or ranges, and it seems to me it would be the part of wisdom to include cooking ranges as well as furnaces. I should like to ask the minister if he will consider that point.

The line has to be drawn somewhere, and the moment one gets into stoves he has to consider electric ranges and then other electrical equipment for the house. It was not thought desirable to go into that phase of it.

Also
electric fans.

I should like to say a word in regard to that. I still think it would be only a matter of justice if cooking ranges were included as well as furnaces. In regard to equipment such as electric lighting plants, it seems to me imperative that this provision should apply also. I am thinking now of the farmers out in the country who have not access to hydro power; indeed I know of many farmers who have the hydro running past their doors, but because of the cost of reducing stations and so on they are unable to take advantage of it. Some of these farmers, interested in bettering their home conditions, have purchased little power plants to make their own electricity. It seems to me it would be only a matter of justice and, if I might call it that, a gesture to the farming community, if farm lighting plants were exempted also.
Electric fixtures are not included in this list of exemptions.

I was going on to deal
with that. I should like to suggest that farm lighting plants be exempted from the sales tax. If you have a farm lighting plant, of necessity you will have some lighting equipment, and I would suggest that the lighting equipment entering into not only the homes of farmers but also the homes of those in the cities be exempted from the sales tax. I feel that this would give a real stimulus to better home conditions, and now that we have gone this far it seems to me that we should go all the way in that regard and remove
lighting equipment and farm lighting plants from under the sales tax. I think we should also include ranges along with furnaces.

Members of the committee have not a copy of the amendments. I should like to know whether or not the materials that go into the manufacture of paint, varnishes, white lead and paint oil are exempt from sales tax.
Yes.
And also the raw materials that go into the manufacture of furnaces for heating purposes?
Yes, for heating buildings.
How are you going to determine that when you are in your foundry casting them? That is what the hon. member for Kootenay East pointed out, namely, that it is too complicated.
Just let me meet that point. If part of the furnaces are taxable, the materials are free; and now for these furnaces that are not taxable the materials are being made free, so there is no difficulty.

How are you going to differentiate between materials for a given purpose that are free, and materials that are not? For instance, in this steel item we are freeing structural steel for bridges. Clearly that has nothing to do with the building program; but it is quite obvious that if you are going to do that, you should also free reinforcing steel, which might enter into a concrete building, whereas the other might not have anything to do with building at all.
I am informed that it is included in structural steel.

This is the first time I have ever heard of that. If you go down to the customs house and try to get it through, you will find that it is not. Just take your bundle of rods down there and try to get them through; then take your structural steel and try to get it through, and see whether they are in the same class.

The item is " structural
steel to 'be used exclusively for the framework and supports of buildings and bridges."

Exactly, and that is
structural steel; that does not cover reinforcing rods.

I do not wish to appear insistent, but I should like the minister to give me a definite opinion in regard to the suggestions I have made.
Special War Revenue Act

My feeling is that this is quite a long list as it is, and the matter of where the line should be drawn has been very carefully considered. The hon. gentleman has suggested that we should move into the realm of stoves, which would get us into electric ranges and even, as one hon. member suggested, electric fans and electrical equipment generally. It is not considered desirable to do that; it would take us into too large a field of exemption. The other request of the hon. member was that lighting equipment for farmers' houses should be included; but I would point out to him that there is no exemption of electrical fixtures or any lighting equipment, so far as I can see, and while it would be very nice not to pay sales tax rather than pay it on a wide range of articles, still I do not see why we should extend this list.

I should like to support the hon. member for Portage la Prairie. I believe that if the minister will consider the matter from this point of view, that rural houses must have electric lighting equipment, such as the Delco lighting system-
Largely sold in the west.

Yes; it is sold largely in the west. I take it that this scheme for the construction of lower priced houses is designed to assist not only the people who live in towns and cities but also those who live in the rural communities.
The town dweller does not get any exemption on his lighting equipment.
But the town dweller simply runs a wire into his house.
But he pays for his lighting, and that charge covers the cost of some lighting equipment on which there is no exemption.

Nevertheless the additional outlay in regard to the lighting equipment in the rural house is almost prohibitive, and when the sales tax is added it greatly increases the cost of installation. I agree with the hon, member for Portage la Prairie that people living on farms are entitled to consideration because of the disadvantages which they suffer in regard to the hook-up that is necessary to connect them to the hydro or, as in Saskatchewan, to the lines running out from the steam plants in the cities. In my opinion the request of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie would be simply a matter of justice to a large number of people who suffer many inconveniences that most of us do not suffer. I think the same applies to heating equipment. The cheaper houses, particularly in the country 
places, are often, on account of fuel difficulties, heated by stoves, and I think the rural population is entitled to consideration in this regard. I would very strongly support the hon. member for Portage la Prairie in his request, not that action be taken to-night but that the matter be considered carefully before a definite answer is given.

I am disposed
to agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and the hon. member for Portage la Prairie. If people in isolated houses want these advantages, they are compelled to pay about nine times what they would cost an individual in an urban area, where he can get his lighting connection for an expenditure of about $30 or $40. The farmer has to pay about $400 or $500 for equipment which would bring about the same results. That point really requires some consideration.

I understand the point of
view taken by the hon. member, but I do not think we can possibly do what hon. members are asking without exempting the whole range of electrical fixtures and lighting equipment generally. I do not see how we can possibly draw the line where the hon. member suggests it should be drawn. Certainly it would entail a very serious loss of revenue. We would go from electrical fixtures to lamps and lanterns, and everything pertaining to lighting.
With regard to stoves I must say that they are not part of a building. They are not fixtures, whereas furnaces are. Furnaces are installed as part of a property, and it seems to me that for the reasons I stated before it would be very difficult to draw the line.

May I point out again
that the minister would not be entering the realm of lighting fixtures if he were to exempt a lighting plant. The sale of a lighting plant is something entirely by itself, and includes an engine and installation. That is all they charge for.
And batteries.

Yes, if you need batteries. The engine and batteries constitute the lighting equipment. Anything else would be extra, and it would not come under the heading of lighting. So, if the lighting plants were exempted on farm houses, it seems to me we would simply be carrying out a matter of justice. I can speak from experience. I have been used to electric lights on the farm, and I know, when we installed one about twenty years ago, before we got through with the installation it cost about $1,600 to get the plant. On the other hand, as one

Special War Revenue Act
hon. member has pointed out, in the city all one would have to do would be to attach a wire. Upkeep, refueling and that sort of thing cost a considerable amount of money every year; I know whereof I speak.
At the present time one can buy the Delco lighting plant for $647.50, and that is just the start of the expense in connection with the equipping of farm houses with electric lights and electric power. I have risen to say that we can certainly draw a distinction between a lighting plant and lighting fixtures. Again I say it is only a matter of justice that farm lighting plants be exempted from the sales tax.

Are the lightning rods
used on rural buildings exempt from the sales tax?
No; they are not included.
Would this include metal as well as wooden sash? I notice we mention metal lath as well as wooden lath.
It includes both.
Then there should be some change, and metal siding should be included as well.

It includes all lath and
sash.

Why are pipes
and fittings not exempt? They enter very largely into the hot water heating systems of houses.
Because they are put to so many other uses. That is the reason why they are not included.

Then the commercial heaters which are used to such a great extent in England enter into the picture, so far as small houses are concerned. I believe they are manufactured, by the McClary Company. They take the place of furnaces, and are permanent fixtures in houses. Cannot something be done to have more than furnaces included?
All these houses have hot water heating equipment, and that equipment is just as much a part of the building and is just as necessary a part as is the furnace. Surely hot water heating equipment is part of a building, and it seems to me it should be included in the exemptions.

I think the term "furnaces" should be clarified right now. The use of the word "furnace" is not sufficient. Probably it should mention hot air furnaces and hot water furnaces. I would not suggest
steam equipment, because it is used only in the large plants, and is not necessary in the smaller type of houses it is here intended to help. But hot water furnaces are being put in small houses of the type indicated, and are installed for about $350.

Hot water furnaces are
included.
With pipes, complete?
No, no pipes or radiators.
Pipes are not included?
No.
Are you putting down hot water furnaces only?
All furnaces.

All furnaces, without
pipes?
Yes.

I think something should be done about the matter of furnaces. For instance, every house has a domestic hot water heating plant. Every large building has that type of heating plant. They are very expensive, and the sales tax on such a plant amounts to quite a large sum. I should think it would be just as important to eliminate the sales tax on that plant as to eliminate it on any other building material. I think, further, that in order to make the matter clear we ought to mention metal sash and wooden sash.
No; that would limit it.

I should like to add my voice to what was said by hon. members in this part of the chamber and by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie with regard to the lighting system in farm houses. I believe farmers will feel that discrimination has been exercised against them if they are not given the same consideration. We distinctly wish to help farming communities and to make living conditions on the farm worth while. If they did not take advantage of the situation, it would be their own fault, and they would have themselves to blame. I believe the government would be well advised to consider the farmers, and to eliminate the eight per cent sales tax so far as lighting systems in farm houses are concerned.

Nearly everything which
enters into the construction of a farm house is covered by this list. It includes lumber, sash, doors, shingles, paint, glass and so on.
Special War Revenue Act

The lighting system is something which is very necessary on a farm. Although conditions may be different in the east, I know that in western Canada, and particularly in Saskatchewan, very few farm houses are adjacent to power lines. Consequently, modern installations in new houses require systems of the type we have been discussing. If the minister could see his way clear to recommend the addition, I am sure it would be greatly appreciated.

Do the exemptions in the
schedule apply for any purpose whatsoever.

I do not understand the
question.
I am asking if the goods exempted in the schedule can be utilized for any purpose whatsoever?
Yes.
I notice that an exemption is allowed only for glass used for building purposes, but it would seem that other goods so exempted could be used for purposes other than building.
Does the hon. member refer to furnaces?
Hardware such as locks and hinges do not necessarily have to be utilized for building purposes.
Most of these can be used only in connection with buildings, for example, roofings.
Pulleys would not have to be used on buildings, and there are other items of hardware that could be used for other purposes. Why should this exemption not apply to items used for other purposes?
The bon. member is not suggesting that we should exempt glass dishes, for instance?
Glass can ibe used for many other purposes, and I do not see why we should exempt it for buildings only.
Glass has so many uses that it is necessary to restrict it.
That would include plate glass?
Yes.

A few days ago a deputation of four or five large manufacturers of builders' hardware came to Ottawa and made mention of several items that had been left
[Mr. Ilslcy.)
out of this list which they considered were just as essential as some of those that are included. Have those items been included?

No. I think those manufacturers of builders' hardware suggested that the enumeration should be left out and that all builders' hardware should be exempted. That covered such a tremendous range that we did not think we could do it. Their main difficulty was in connection with materials, and that is covered by the amendment.

If I remember correctly, the list does not include handles used for raising window sash. In other words, one can get the window down but would find it impossible to get it up. That leaves one in a rather awkward position.

I have not a copv of the amendment before me, and I should like to understand exactly what it covers. Hot water and steam boilers are now exempt from this tax. Would that apply to old buildings as well as to new?
Yes.

Radiators are not
exempt from the tax. Are all the materials entering into the manufacture of steam boilers and radiators exempt from the tax?
All that enter into the construction of furnaces for the heating of buildings. Radiators are not exempt.
Previously materials entering into the manufacture of radiators were exempt from the tax.
Radiators are taxable.
Would the minister care to express an opinion as to whether reinforcing steel used to reinforce concrete in constructing buildings and bridges will come within the term "structural steel"?
All I can say is that it is intended to be included. Before the bill is brought down, I shall consult with the officials to see that there is no doubt about the point.
I want to thank the government for bringing in this amendment.

Now that bridges have been added to the resolution is it quite clear that this item will cover all steel used in the construction of a bridge, such as foundation steel, main girders, cross girders and bearers?

I would think they would all be included.

Special War Revenue Act

I understand instructions have been given to cancel licences which have been granted to manufacturers of paint and to those engaged in the industrial trade. The result is, except in connection with certain items, that manufacturers of paint will have to pay the eight per cent sales tax on their ingredients.
Materials are exempted by the amendment.

The paint manufacturers have been granted a broad licence which covers practically all their primary products. The amendment now specifies certain primary products used in the paint manufacturing business, so that all others will be subject to the eight per cent sales tax.
The amendment takes care of the situation referred to by the hon. gentleman. Was the hon. gentleman in the chamber when we were discussing the amendment?
I have been here all evening.
The amendment covers all materials entering into the manufacture of paints, varnishes, white lead and paint oil.
All the primary products of a paint manufacturer will be free?
But not to include materials consumed by waste or wear or abrasives.
Materials entering into the manufacture of paint?
Yes.

An industrialist who buys large quantities of paint may still have his licence to buy that paint free from sales tax? For instance, a manufacturer of a household article may buy a large quantity of paint to use in finishing his product. Will he still be able to buy that paint free of the eight per cent sales tax?
Yes.
His previous licence has not been revoked?
He will not need to use his licence, because hereafter all paint is to be free.
Even though it is not used in connection with building?
It is free for any purpose.

I communicated with the
minister to ask that rock asphalt should be included in the items to be exempted from the sales tax. This material is being used in the construction of concrete buildings and for
the fire-proofing of buildings. The minister told me that this matter would be considered, and I should like to know if it is covered by the amendment.
Will the hon. gentleman let that stand until I find out just what is rock asphalt?

I notice that builders' hardware is exempted, but no mention is made of nails and spikes. They are a most important item, especially in building small buildings. A small building can be constructed without a furnace or radiator, but it would need a considerable quantity of nails.
They are used for so many other purposes.
The two and a half, three, four and even six inch nails are practically all used in building construction. I wish the minister would consider this item.

A paint manufacturer sells probably 65 per cent of his production to the industrial trade, the balance going to the retailer. Will he have to charge the eight per cent sales tax on what he sells to the retail merchant?
Paint is free for all purposes.
It has not been in the past.
That is what we are doing now.

What is going to happen to the retail merchant who may have stocked up a month previously? The public are naturally expecting a reduction in the price of paint, but the retail merchant has already secured his supply and paid his eight per cent sales tax. Will any consideration be given to the retail merchants in that position from one end of Canada to the other? They have prepared for the season's trade and paid the eight per cent sales tax, and customers coming in wanting to buy paint will say, "Why should not paint be lower by eight or ten per cent, now the budget has gone through?" Will any allowance be made for the stocks on hand in the retail stores, or will anything be done to meet that situation?

That was very carefully considered, and it was thought that we could not provide for any refund. When the sales tax was being increased there was an appreciation in the value of retail stocks, and the retailer got the advantage of that. Now that the taxes are reduced, there are instances where he will suffer a depreciation of his stock.
Special War Revenue Act

I venture to suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the retail merchant is already provided for, because when prices are brought down by the removal of the tax there will be an increased volume of trade which will amply provide for the additional profits the retailer desires to secure. The retail merchant will also receive an additional volume of sales as a result of the building program which this parliament is putting through.

Yes. I think the retailers of builders' supplies will be glad to have this done, for the reason mentioned by my hon. friend, even though they may have stocks on hand on which they may have paid the tax.
Do I understand there will be no rebate of sales taxes which have already been paid?
There will be no rebates.
With regard to furnaces for heating buildings, there are in my constituency buildings for the curing of tobacco which are heated by furnaces. Will these furnaces be exempt?
They are for the curing of tobacco.

But also for the heating of the building. There was also an appeal to the minister for the exemption of the sales tax on oil burners used for the same purpose, and I was wondering if he had given consideration to that.
Consideration has been given.
If structural steel used in bridges is exempt, is it also exempt in the construction of industrial plants?
For buildings and bridges.

Perhaps one of the most essential things in a low rental house is the electric wiring and the fuses and switches that go with the wiring. These are just as essential as the paint. Is provision made for their exemption?
There is no provision made for exempting wire. Wiring has a very wide range of use, and it was not thought desirable to include it.

I am still of the opinion that there are certain items of builders' finishing hardware which it is essential to include in the exemptions. Would the minister be good enough to let the item stand over until the next sitting?

The question can be raised
on the bill. This is merely the resolution, and there will be a bill before us later.
In every community there is a wall paper business. Just to clarify the item, would the minister say whether that is included?
Wall paper is included in the list of exemptions.

Item agreed to.
Amendment agreed to.
Paragraph as amended agreed to.
2.	That schedule II to the said act be amended by striking out the following words in paragraph three thereof:
Provided that the tax hereby imposed shall not apply to the goods mentioned herein, when sold to or imported by manufacturers of automobiles or chassis for the original equipment of such automobiles or chassis under the following conditions:
(i)	If less than ten thousand automobiles or chassis are manufactured or produced per annum and at least fifty per centum of the factory cost of manufacturing or producing them, exclusive of duties and other taxes, is incurred in the British Empire;
(ii)	If ten thousand automobiles or chassis or more are manufactured or produced per annum and at least sixty per centum of the factory cost of manufacturing or producing them, exclusive of duties and other taxes, is incurred in the British Empire;
Provided, however, that effective April 1st, 1938, the words "sixty-five" shall be substituted for the word "sixty" in this paragraph, and substituting therefor the following:
Provided that the tax hereby imposed shall not apply to the goods mentioned herein when used exclusively for the original equipment of such automotive vehicles.
Would the minister explain just what this section means before we proceed with it in detail?

At present tires and tubes
are taxable, tires at two cents a pound and tubes at three cents a pound. If they are original equipment on automobiles that have a certain empire content, no tax applies. If the number of automobiles manufactured is 10,000 or under, the empire content has to be 50 per cent; if the number is over 10,000, the content now has to be 65 per cent, formerly 60 per cent. That provision is in one of the schedules of our Special War Revenue Act, and it was to offer an incentive to get a larger empire content. The manufacturers of automobiles that did not have that content, and with tires as part of the original equipment, have to pay on the tires and tubes two cents and three cents a pound. At the time that schedule was drafted it was thought that this

Special War Revenue Act
tax would apply to tires on imported automobiles, but it was discovered that it was not applicable to them.
Because they were covered by the automobile as a whole.

That is correct, but there
is another reason too. The result was that the tire manufacturers in Canada found themselves at a great disadvantage in trying to sell tires for imported automobiles.

Because they already
had the tires on.

The imported automobile
came in with the foreign tires on tax-free, so there was no reason why it should have a Canadian tire. This provision gives the Canadian manufacturer of tires a chance on that business.

When you import an
automobile with four wheels, it has four tires, I should think. It would not come in as an automobile without the tires on the wheels?
Oh, yes, it is a business practice to import automobiles without tires. There is a guarantee which is of value that goes with Canadian tires, and Canadians want Canadian tires.
This would have to be computed at the end of each year because it is the yearly production of 10,000 or more.
We do not have to concern ourselves with that now. We did have to concern ourselves with it, and that was an administrative difficulty which is now removed.

Paragraph agreed to.
3.	That subsection two of section fifty-eight of the said act be amended to provide that the excise tax payable upon the sale, transfer or assignment of any share at a price or valuation of one dollar shall be one-quarter of one cent per share.
Paragraph agreed to.
4.	That any enactment founded on this resolution shall be deemed to have come into force on the seventeenth day of June, one thousand nine hundred and thirty-eight and to have applied to all goods imported or taken out of warehouse for consumption on and after that date and to have applied to goods previously imported for which no entry for consumption was made before that date.

There is a difficulty about section 4, because of the amendment which was made in connection with steel. Is that to be covered also? Under section 3 of the resolution, the rate is a quarter of a cent. What was the old rate?
This affects only shares of exactly one dollar. The present rate is one-tenth of one per cent. This is one-quarter of a cent.
As regards steel, I am thinking about the question of rebates that was mentioned by the minister.
I think it can be administered if we leave the date the seventeenth day of June, even for structural steel.
I take it that there will have to be a rebate.
Adjustments will have to be made.
Paragraph agreed to.

The resolution is carried, I
believe.
Yes.

Resolution agreed to.
